design-status.name: README/design-status-01
design-status.text: These documents record the adopted design and name the decisions still needed for a concrete protocol. The executable design candidate has 105 proved declarations — 84 for the registry, 7 for the naming instance, 9 for its lifecycle and 5 for its wire encoding, counts that the model check derives from the theorem manifests — plus a playable simulation transcribed from them. The focused checks replay 29 registry rows, 15 naming rows and 21 lifecycle rows; they test correspondence on those finite inputs rather than proving browser behaviour generally. No independent audit acceptance is claimed. The compiled validators and a registry deployed on the public preprod network are recorded in the preprod record, and the conformance evidence states which consumer requirements a named code revision demonstrated against them. The coverage ledger distinguishes finite executable evidence from conditions, abstractions and omissions, and the clarity record states plainly how much independence that evidence has.

design-status.name: README/design-status-02
design-status.text: The Nix-built documentation archive is a review bundle, not a released protocol artifact. It contains the rendered site and a runnable, locked workspace with raw model and corpus files, the naming contract, scenarios, simulator and replay sources, checkers, and exact identities. Reproduction starts from a fresh extraction, verifies artifacts/SHA256SUMS, and runs the archive's own flake; a checkout pass does not substitute. Build and release details give the exact commands and describe the release pipeline that publishes the archive from a tag on main.

design-status.name: README/design-status-03
design-status.text: Singular uses MPF as its authenticated registry data structure. The product it was imported from is a separate application with potentially reusable mechanics. The implementation stack and shared-library boundaries remain unselected; extracting a shared library is future work.

design-status.name: README/design-status-04
design-status.text: Build and serve the documentation with the pinned Nix toolchain.

how-the-parts-fit.name: README/how-the-parts-fit-01
how-the-parts-fit.text: The diagram and table in this section record the original three-operation design: Insert, Update and Delete requests, an application-minted Withdraw, and the states Absent, Active and Over. The registry-mode model that the Lean proves, the simulator replays and the conformance suite compares against the deployed validators supports registration and permanent termination, and calls the terminal state Terminal. The original design below is historical; the active permanent contract contract rejects the other five edge encodings: how a name moves in the registry shows the encoded edges and permanent contract admission, and the model ledger records what replaced each part of the original design.

how-the-parts-fit.name: README/how-the-parts-fit-02
how-the-parts-fit.text: The application keeps its state in the UTxO holding the NFT and controls its own local transitions; the registry never sees that state. Singular records only whether a key has an outstanding representative or has been permanently retired, and enforces the coupling between registry transitions and NFT supply.

how-the-parts-fit.name: README/how-the-parts-fit-03
how-the-parts-fit.text: Active and Over contain no application payload. Registry Update means retirement, not an application-state update. Over is terminal.

how-the-parts-fit.name: README/how-the-parts-fit-04
how-the-parts-fit.text: The configured application policy ID is the authorization anchor. It mints action tokens whose asset names hash the action and its necessary parameters. Insert approval binds the registry/key, initial application datum and destination. Withdraw approval separately binds the exact pending Insert and its refund requirements; Insert approval alone cannot authorize cancellation.

how-the-parts-fit.name: README/how-the-parts-fit-05
how-the-parts-fit.text: Insert carries no representative NFT, can fail at folding if its key is occupied, and can be withdrawn with the required authorization. Update/Delete carry the existing representative after the application authorizes its exact release, and retain it until completion. The concrete request-token arrangement for Update/Delete remains open.

how-the-parts-fit.name: README/how-the-parts-fit-06
how-the-parts-fit.text: Read the design in order. The first three pages and the protocol specification record the original design; the naming pages and the simulation describe the registry-mode model that supersedes it where they differ.

how-the-parts-fit.text: Naming: book a name, retire it, attest it

how-the-parts-fit.name: README/how-the-parts-fit-12
how-the-parts-fit.text: Ending a name and recovering control on a real ledger

how-the-parts-fit.text: Draft protocol specification and acceptance scenarios

install.name: README/install-01
install.text: From the release after 0.13.1, without Nix. On a Mac with Apple Silicon:

install.name: README/install-02
install.text: On Linux on x86_64, download singular-X.Y.Z-x86_64-linux.deb or singular-X.Y.Z-x86_64-linux.rpm from the releases page and install it with your package manager, or run the AppImage of a command. Each of them gives singular, open-datum and devnet, the private development node Demo 1 starts, and, except the AppImages, the deployment blueprint the commands take as --blueprint. The install page has the commands, the checksums and the tarballs that hold all three in one folder.

singular.name: README/singular-01
singular.text: A permissionless registry on Cardano for unique identities and independent application state.

start-here-play-demo-1.name: README/start-here-play-demo-1-01
start-here-play-demo-1.text: As a Cardano developer who knows cardano-cli, wallets, faucets and Koios but not Singular, you can play Demo 1, a registry from creation to termination in sixteen steps, and watch every step either succeed or be refused where the page says it will. The Demo 1 page says what the play shows and where to play it: the step-by-step page of singular-demo, with a copy button on every block; its Nix shell, which holds singular, open-datum and a private development chain; and its Ubuntu kit for a machine without Nix. To play it in a browser with nothing installed, open the Killercoda scenario; to watch it without running anything, open the recorded run.

start-here-play-demo-1.name: README/start-here-play-demo-1-02
start-here-play-demo-1.text: Try the simulation — register a name, terminate it permanently, and inspect refusals for the five historical edge encodings. Switch the profile picker to the naming instance for the Over witness and the lifecycle replay. The simulation guide says what the page establishes and what it does not.

who-this-is-for.name: README/who-this-is-for-00
who-this-is-for.text: Who this is for.

who-this-is-for.name: README/who-this-is-for-01
who-this-is-for.text: An application developer wants keys that are unique across everyone using the application — names, identifiers, handles — without running a registrar. They supply one parameter, their application policy ID, and get a registry in which every active key is represented by exactly one NFT sitting in one of their own application outputs. Singular mints that NFT when a certified registration is folded in, burns it when the key is retired or released, and lets a released key be registered again.

who-this-is-for.name: README/who-this-is-for-02
who-this-is-for.text: A user of that application asks it to register a key. The application approves the exact proposal — including the refund address stored in the request — and the request waits, holding no NFT, until someone folds it into the registry. Before folding, a separately authorized cancellation copies that stored refund address and leaves the name free; redirecting the refund, relying only on Insert certification, cancelling after fold, or replaying cancellation is refused. The registry fixes where a deposit returns, never its amount: no fee, price or bond rule is part of it.

who-this-is-for.name: README/who-this-is-for-03
who-this-is-for.text: A holder of an active name wants to keep payment routing current, recover through a committed next controller, or retire the name permanently. The naming lifecycle covers destination maintenance, recovery through the committed key, and retirement by that key or by a distinct-member quorum — never by the current control key alone. Twenty-one lifecycle rows are replayed in the simulator against the Lean that computed them. It remains an unaccepted design candidate, not an observed ledger execution.

who-this-is-for.name: README/who-this-is-for-04
who-this-is-for.text: A folder — anyone at all — collects pending requests and applies them to the registry in one transaction. There is no owner to sign, no privileged actor, and no way to fold a request that does not satisfy the protocol.

who-this-is-for.name: README/who-this-is-for-05
who-this-is-for.text: A resolver wants to know whether a key is active and where its application state currently lives. It authenticates the registry entry, finds the NFT, and reads the application's own output. A key that is retired or in a pending terminal request yields no live state.

who-this-is-for.name: README/who-this-is-for-06
who-this-is-for.text: A Cardano developer who wants to try it plays the whole thing on a private test chain from a page of steps to copy, signing with a vault wallet whose key stays sealed in a file on their machine, or signing on another machine. The Demo 1 page says what the play shows and links the steps.

archived-broader-model-evidence.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/archived-broader-model-evidence-01
archived-broader-model-evidence.text: A proof is only worth what its statement says. This page reads the registry-mode model back in English — what each promise actually quantifies over, what it assumes, and where the reader should not take it further than it goes — so that "proved" can be checked against "promised" without reading Lean.

archived-broader-model-evidence.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/archived-broader-model-evidence-02
archived-broader-model-evidence.text: The statements themselves, with their digests, are in the theorem manifest. This page is about their meaning.

how-much-independence-this-record-has.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/how-much-independence-this-record-has-00
how-much-independence-this-record-has.text: How much independence this record has.

how-much-independence-this-record-has.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/how-much-independence-this-record-has-01
how-much-independence-this-record-has.text: Stated plainly, because a reader cannot see it from the outside: the model, the corpus generator, the simulator transcription and this readback all have the same author.

how-much-independence-this-record-has.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/how-much-independence-this-record-has-02
how-much-independence-this-record-has.text: That has a concrete consequence. A misunderstanding of the interface made while writing the model will be made again while transcribing it and again while reading it back, and none of the three will catch it — they are not independent measurements, they are one measurement repeated. What the internal machinery does catch is real but narrower: transcription slips (the corpus replay), statements that do not constrain what they appear to (the mutation record), unproved obligations (the compiled axiom check), and drift between the shipped Lean and the built Lean (the mirror check).

how-much-independence-this-record-has.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/how-much-independence-this-record-has-03
how-much-independence-this-record-has.text: The check this record cannot perform on itself is the one that matters most — whether the statements say what the interface promised. That requires someone who did not write them. Treat this page as the author's best account, written to be falsifiable, and not as an audit.

lean-clarity-record.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/lean-clarity-record-01
lean-clarity-record.text: As a reader of current permanent contract, I can register a fresh key and terminate it permanently. The active model and compiled state support exactly tags 1 (insertActive) and 3 (updateTerminal); tags 0, 2, 4, 5 and 6 are explicitly refused, including caller-constructed and mixed requests. Application payload maintenance is separate. Current sources and receipts must be bound to the revised candidate.

lean-clarity-record.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/lean-clarity-record-02
lean-clarity-record.text: The detailed walkthrough and measurements below are archived broader model evidence, retained to explain the earlier contract; their broader success claims do not apply to permanent contract. Historical sources are retained on preserve/m2/pre-m1-source-removal. The active theorem manifest and the exact scope-retirement record explain the changed law and denominator. Unmet consumer requirements stay uncovered.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-01
reading-the-promises-back.text: No tree change without approval (no_tree_change_without_approval). If a request is accepted and it is not the read, then an approval was present, it was minted under the registry's own pinned policy, its asset name is the hash of the edge, the key, the owner and the destination of this request, and the registry's own pins — its policy, its owner, its recovery commitment — are unchanged by the fold. The part worth dwelling on: a correct policy is necessary and not sufficient. An approval minted for a different key, or a different destination, under the very same policy, does not admit the request. A model that checked only the policy would be wrong in a way no amount of proving would reveal, which is why the tuple appears in the statement rather than in a comment.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-02
reading-the-promises-back.text: Booked at most once (booked_at_most_once). A batch is a fold, and the fold spends each request once, in order. The statement is about the step function, so a request cannot be applied twice within one batch, and a batch that fails anywhere produces no state at all rather than a partial one.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-03
reading-the-promises-back.text: Permanence (terminal_attestation_permanent). A terminated key stays terminated through any later sequence of accepted folds. A terminal leaf has no outgoing edge, so nothing downstream can make the termination false. This is the promise that lets a reader keep the leaf it proved rather than re-reading the chain.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-04
reading-the-promises-back.text: The supply law (biconditional_supply_sync). For every key in a reachable state, the count of outstanding active tokens is one exactly when the leaf is active and zero otherwise — a biconditional, both directions, over all keys, not only the key in hand. This is the statement that ties the token supply to the map and makes "the token is the name" more than a slogan.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-05
reading-the-promises-back.text: Occupancy and its converse (occupancy, occupancy_free_key_succeeds). A booking edge succeeds only on a key that is not already taken; and on a key that is free, with a matching approval, it does succeed. The converse matters as much as the rule: a registry that refused everything would satisfy the first half perfectly.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-06
reading-the-promises-back.text: Termination (termination). On a terminal key every leaf-moving edge is refused. Not "should be", not "by convention" — the refusal is the complement of the edge table, so there is no unlisted case that quietly moves a retired name.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-07
reading-the-promises-back.text: The witness law (active_witness_unique). At most one active token per key, and exactly one when the leaf is active.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-08
reading-the-promises-back.text: The seven inversions. For each edge, a single statement saying what an accepted application of it did: the leaf before, the leaf after, the new root, the token deltas, the custody movement, the deposit destination. These are the statements the simulator is really transcribing, and they are the ones to read first when asking whether the model matches the interface, because they contain no reachability hypothesis to hide behind.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-09
reading-the-promises-back.text: The deposit (inside update_active_inversion and delete_absent_inversion). The two edges that consume an absent witness pay the deposit back to the refund address the original request named, not to the output of the consuming request and not to whoever folded it. Those two rejected destinations are the reason the statement pins the address rather than merely asserting that some payment occurred.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-10
reading-the-promises-back.text: The read (read_changes_nothing, witness_terminal_inversion). An accepted read leaves the leaf, the root and custody exactly as they were and adds one terminal token. It needs no approval at all — and, symmetrically, a stray approval does not make it refuse.

reading-the-promises-back.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/reading-the-promises-back-11
reading-the-promises-back.text: The fold (empty_fold_error, fold_batch_cons). An empty batch is refused rather than accepted as a no-op. A non-empty batch succeeds exactly when its head applies and the rest applies to the result, which is what makes a batch mean the same thing as the sequence of its requests.

the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over-00
the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over.text: The shape the promises are made over.

the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over-01
the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over.text: Almost every promise is stated over reachable states — genesis, closed under accepted folds — and not over arbitrary values of the state type. This is not a weakening dressed up as a hypothesis: over an arbitrary state value the supply laws are false, because nothing stops you writing down a state with three active tokens for one key. Reachability is what makes them true, and it is exactly the property a chain enforces by only ever arriving at a state through a fold.

the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over-02
the-shape-the-promises-are-made-over.text: Where a promise does not need reachability, it does not assume it. The seven inversions, the empty-batch refusal, the fold-cons equation and read_changes_nothing are proved over any state at all, because they are statements about what an accepted edge did, not about what the ledger holds.

what-is-bound.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/what-is-bound-01
what-is-bound.text: Every one of these ships beside the page under simulator/formal/, and node simulator/mirror-check.mjs fails if the shipped copy and the built copy differ, in either direction. Changing any bound input invalidates this record.

what-is-bound.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/what-is-bound-02
what-is-bound.text: The readback below covers the eleven promises, the seven inversions, the deposit, the read and the fold. The registry module bound above also carries fifteen later statements — about when a pending request may be retracted and what a refused retraction is told, what every exit pays and to whom, and which datum a delivered or spent witness carries, and how a batch of one folds — that are listed in the theorem manifest and not yet read back here.

what-the-model-does-not-say.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/what-the-model-does-not-say-00
what-the-model-does-not-say.text: What the model does not say.

what-the-model-does-not-say.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/what-the-model-does-not-say-01
what-the-model-does-not-say.text: These are limits of the model, not gaps in the proofs. Each is a place where a reader could reasonably expect more than is there.

what-the-model-does-not-say.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/what-the-model-does-not-say-02
what-the-model-does-not-say.text: The last row is the important one. Everything on this page is about a model. Whether the deployed validator implements it is a different question with a different kind of evidence behind it, and this page is not that evidence.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/who-this-is-for-00
who-this-is-for.text: Who this is for.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-LEAN-CLARITY/who-this-is-for-01
who-this-is-for.text: A reviewer deciding whether the model is the right model. The build already answers are these proved — every one is, from the standard axioms and nothing else. It cannot answer do these say what the interface promised, and that is the question this page exists to make answerable.

build-and-check.name: docs-building/build-and-check-02
build-and-check.text: The documentation package and checks use the locked shared MkDocs toolchain. The documentation check inspects rendered internal links, section anchors, navigation, speech data and theme assets. Separate model and simulator checks exercise the proved Lean model and its finite corpus, and the model check cross-checks the compiled axiom report against the theorem manifest; none proves application behavior. See the model ledger and simulation for their exact scope.

build-and-check.name: docs-building/build-and-check-03
build-and-check.text: The browser check launches the pinned Chromium build, serves the standalone simulator on a temporary loopback port, and executes its manual-control and story assertions. The canonical runner is tools/browser-check.mjs; the earlier callback under simulator/ is retained as historical browser evidence. Screenshots use a temporary writable directory; no browser download or external service is required during execution. Set KEEP_BROWSER_EVIDENCE=1 to retain successful browser evidence. CI's build gate realizes the packages, executing checks, and development-shell inputs before the downstream verification jobs.

building-the-documentation.name: docs-building/building-the-documentation-01
building-the-documentation.text: The site renders the repository's canonical Markdown and specification. A generated staging directory preserves their relative paths; it is not a second editable documentation tree.

documentation-releases.name: docs-building/documentation-releases-01
documentation-releases.text: The documentation version is the one version.txt, the release manifest and the changelog agree on; a prepared version is not evidence that an archive was tagged or published. Release-please's simple strategy updates those three surfaces together for later versions, and Nix requires the version and manifest to agree. These are documentation versions, not deployed protocol versions.

documentation-releases.name: docs-building/documentation-releases-02
documentation-releases.text: After a successful main-branch gate, repository-scoped App credentials let release-please prepare a release PR whose changes trigger normal CI. It plans PRs only: release creation is disabled because upstream release creation posts a PR comment. Merging the release PR prepares the version but does not tag or publish it. An operator-authorized v<version> tag on that merged release PR's exact commit triggers publication. The commit must belong to main, and tag, manifest and version must agree.

documentation-releases.name: docs-building/documentation-releases-03
documentation-releases.text: The tag workflow builds and checks a Nix-produced documentation archive and checksum, publishes them to the matching GitHub release, downloads and verifies the uploaded bytes, then changes the release PR's pending label to tagged. It accepts a pending or already-tagged matching PR so interrupted publication can be retried. It does not post PR comments. CI has a manual recovery trigger; no release workflow or tag is dispatched merely by adding this automation.

documentation-releases.name: docs-building/documentation-releases-04
documentation-releases.text: Build the documentation archive locally with nix build .#docs-release, and run version, workflow and artifact checks with nix run .#release-check. The archive contains the rendered site and speech data plus a complete review workspace under artifacts/review/: model and theorem sources, finite corpora, scenarios, simulator and replay sources, checkers, and a minimal flake with its exact lock. The inner artifacts/SHA256SUMS authenticates every review input plus the separately served corpus and identity files; the outer SHA256SUMS authenticates the archive.

documentation-releases.name: docs-building/documentation-releases-05
documentation-releases.text: Packaging checks alone do not establish reproduction. Extract the built singular-docs-<version>.tar.gz into a fresh directory, change to that directory, run sha256sum --check artifacts/SHA256SUMS, then run nix run --no-write-lock-file ./artifacts/review#check. Nix may acquire the exact locked toolchain when it is not cached; the model, scenario, simulator, replay, checker, and configuration inputs all come from the archive. Provenance comes from the validated tag and build binding. Published releases, each produced by this workflow from a tag on main, are listed at https://github.com/lambdasistemi/singular/releases.

documentation-releases.name: docs-building/documentation-releases-06
documentation-releases.text: The initial empty-manifest behavior and version override follow the release-please manifest documentation. Publishing remains a separate action from reviewing this documentation.

edit-and-serve.name: docs-building/edit-and-serve-01
edit-and-serve.text: The development shell has a separate CI build because packaged builds do not exercise it:

edit-and-serve.name: docs-building/edit-and-serve-02
edit-and-serve.text: just build-docs and just serve-docs stage the generated API references from the packaged site build, nix build .#docs, so the local site links the same generated pages the packaged site and its checks carry; the Markdown pages still reload live as they are edited.

edit-and-serve.name: docs-building/edit-and-serve-03
edit-and-serve.text: To serve the packaged output without a live-reload editor, run the docs-serve tool (marked not-a-guarantee) with the port as its argument and open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

generated-api-references.name: docs-building/generated-api-references-01
generated-api-references.text: The site ships a generated reference for each library a contributor calls into, built from the same revision as the pages that link it. Which code has one, and what stands in for it where there is none:

generated-api-references.name: docs-building/generated-api-references-02
generated-api-references.text: Executables, test suites and the runtime service modules outside the library's extent have no generated pages here. That coverage gap stays visible, exactly as the off-chain reference's own page records it: wider generated coverage is a separate decision for the epic's owner, not one this page takes. Each generated reference carries a manifest binding its pages to the digests of the source it was generated from, and the documentation check fails when a page, its source or its link targets no longer agree.

haskell-formatting.name: docs-building/haskell-formatting-01
haskell-formatting.text: The repository's Haskell trees are formatted with Fourmolu under one house configuration, fourmolu.yaml at the repository root. Every formatter entrypoint — the off-chain lint check, the Conformance format check and the root recipes below — passes that file explicitly, so a missing configuration fails loudly instead of falling back to Fourmolu's defaults, and there is no per-tree configuration to drift from it.

haskell-formatting.name: docs-building/haskell-formatting-02
haskell-formatting.text: Discovery is dynamic: every Haskell source under offchain/ and conformance/ — the formerly fenced verifier sources and the evaluation spike included — with no directory exclusions, so a new file or component directory is covered with nothing to edit. The Conformance tree gets the same check in its own Nix source context through nix run .#format-check from conformance/ (CI job 'Conformance Haskell format and lint check'). just format-controls runs the negative and positive controls: a source that Fourmolu's defaults accept but the house configuration rejects must fail the check — proving the configuration is read — and its formatter correction must pass it again; a tree without the configuration must fail loudly rather than format with defaults; a newly tracked component tree outside the old directories joins the check through the Git index, while ignored untracked build noise never enters it and a tracked file under an ignored path stays. The controls run over scratch copies and never touch the working tree.

haskell-formatting.name: docs-building/haskell-formatting-03
haskell-formatting.text: HLint runs over the same discovered extent with no exclusions and no ignore file: nix run .#lint from offchain/ (CI job 'Off-chain lint') checks both formats and hints, and nix run .#hlint-check from conformance/ runs beside the Conformance format check.

ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-buil.name: docs-building/ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-builds-00
ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-buil.text: Ordinary binaries and explicit test builds.

ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-buil.name: docs-building/ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-builds-01
ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-buil.text: As a release operator, I build ordinary singular and open-datum with the manual Cabal test-harness flag disabled. Both executable closures use the ordinary registry CLI modules. The release archive and publication commands select these ordinary outputs.

ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-buil.name: docs-building/ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-builds-02
ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-buil.text: As a contributor, I exercise crash windows and provider-answer loss with the separately named test outputs. Their registry CLI modules retain the original hold/drop controls and SINGULAR_HARNESS_TRIE_TRACE, an independent observation of the trie capability's actual operations. That diagnostic is a hidden test input and its evidence belongs to the test build.

ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-buil.name: docs-building/ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-builds-03
ordinary-binaries-and-explicit-test-buil.text: The build control strips and inspects both ordinary compiled executables, reads the actual resolved registry CLI flag, and deliberately rejects the hook-bearing test artifacts and opposite flag polarity. CI runs the ordinary extracted-release journey separately from the test journey's unchanged recovery, race, node-loss and trie-observation assertions. CLI recovery and conformance backend controls select the explicit test composition. The separate replay-fault project remains a deliberately altered test build; its named refusal proof retains its published pending cases. Test outputs are never substituted into the ordinary release verifier or published as ordinary release artifacts.

other-languages.name: docs-building/other-languages-01
other-languages.text: Every other code family the inventory discovers is linted and format-checked by one command, over the inventory's own extent, with the tools the development shell pins:

other-languages.name: docs-building/other-languages-02
other-languages.text: Lean and HTML have no general formatter here, so the explicit style rules are the policy: no tab, no carriage return, no trailing whitespace, and exactly one final newline. Aiken sources are checked by aiken fmt --check inside the onchain/ and naming-onchain/ flake checks, with the Aiken each flake pins; formatting leaves every compiled validator and its hash unchanged. Generated files — the shipped simulator page, the Lean mirror and the cage vectors — are regenerated from their formatted sources, and their freshness checks stay the policy. A code family nobody checks fails just lint instead of passing silently.

publication-and-accessibility.name: docs-building/publication-and-accessibility-01
publication-and-accessibility.text: Pull requests publish to a live preview with the candidate revision recorded alongside the generated site. Preview publication does not post PR comments. The default branch publishes through workflow-mode GitHub Pages after merge; the same documentation build supplies both routes.

publication-and-accessibility.name: docs-building/publication-and-accessibility-02
publication-and-accessibility.text: The Terminal theme follows the system light/dark preference until a reader chooses with the toggle, and remembers that choice. Diagrams follow the same palette and open at full size in a viewer. Each section has a play button that speaks the recorded narration of its paragraphs in the Puck voice. The voice says the page text word for word: the speech companions are written by the extraction tool, which reads the prose of each rendered page, and tables, code blocks and diagrams are not spoken. The documentation check fails when a paragraph changed without its recording. just extract-speech rewrites the companions after a page edit and just narrate records the paragraphs that changed; recording needs a DeepInfra key. Diagrams are Mermaid, rendered by the copy the shared toolchain pins as a fixed-output Nix input and served from the site itself; no page loads a script or stylesheet from outside the site, and the site check fails if one does.

the-repository-code-inventory.name: docs-building/the-repository-code-inventory-01
the-repository-code-inventory.text: just inventory maps every file the tree actually holds to its lint policy and its format policy — or, for data and artifacts, to a named non-code class — and fails on anything unmapped. Discovery walks the tree itself (extensions, shebangs, executable mode and component manifests), so a new source file in a covered directory is mapped without editing anything, while a file nobody classified fails with a named diagnostic instead of passing silently. The same inventory runs over the Nix flake source, where no Git directory exists, through nix run .#inventory-check; pull-request CI runs both forms so the two contexts cannot drift. The checked registry lives in tools/code_inventory.py.

the-repository-code-inventory.name: docs-building/the-repository-code-inventory-02
the-repository-code-inventory.text: The inventory is a mapping, not enforcement: its report names the CI carrier that executes each policy, and every lint and format policy is enforced — no code family is left without a checker, and no source directory is excluded. just inventory-controls runs the negative and positive controls: synthetic orphans injected into scratch copies of the classified tree, each required to produce its intended failure. The controls never touch the working tree.

certification-and-identity-binding.name: docs-certification/certification-and-identity-binding-01
certification-and-identity-binding.text: Historical design. This page records the earlier Insert/Update/Delete design and its broader broader model successor. The active permanent permanent contract model supports only insertActive and updateTerminal. Historical tags 0, 2, 4, 5 and 6 encode refused actions, not available features. Current supported behavior describes permanent contract; archived source and evidence remain on preserve/m2/pre-m1-source-removal.

certification-and-identity-binding.name: docs-certification/certification-and-identity-binding-02
certification-and-identity-binding.text: Singular recognizes native requests. Applications decide whether the requested application behavior is authorized. Insert needs evidence of application approval because there is no existing representative NFT leaving an application UTxO. Update/Delete use the application's authorization of that NFT's transfer into the exact request.

decisions-still-required.name: docs-certification/decisions-still-required-01
decisions-still-required.text: This is an adopted design with unresolved construction details. There is no implementation, completed proof, universal application language or mandatory general-purpose validation plugin in this repository.

policy-and-script-roles.name: docs-certification/policy-and-script-roles-01
policy-and-script-roles.text: The configured application policy ID and an application spending script hash are different roles. One multipurpose script could implement both roles, but sharing a hash is neither required nor forbidden. The same distinction applies to the native policy roles. The eventual implementation must say which roles share code and parameters; this document does not assume separate hashes for all of them.

policy-and-script-roles.name: docs-certification/policy-and-script-roles-02
policy-and-script-roles.text: Writing a policy ID into a request is not enough to make it trusted. The accepted certifier must be authenticated and bound to the registry's rules, so an attacker cannot choose a self-issued certificate. The application policy ID is configured as a Singular parameter; the concrete configuration and binding mechanism remain open. No mandatory global allowlist is selected.

policy-and-script-roles.name: docs-certification/policy-and-script-roles-03
policy-and-script-roles.text: The interface target is one application-specific parameter: the application policy ID. Registry identity and native policy settings are separate protocol configuration. Insert initial state and application destination are approved per-request values, not additional fixed application parameters. This target is not yet proved sufficient for a concrete protocol.

policy-and-script-roles.name: docs-certification/policy-and-script-roles-04
policy-and-script-roles.text: Insert and Withdraw use tokens minted directly under this configured application policy. Singular checks the policy ID and recomputes the action-bound asset name. No second mandatory Singular request policy/token is selected for these actions. Update/Delete retain their NFT-based release authorization; any additional request token or issuer for them remains open.

validation-without-mutable-registry-obse.name: docs-certification/validation-without-mutable-registry-observation-01
validation-without-mutable-registry-obse.text: The configured application minting policy validates application facts, approval and the required construction when it mints the Insert asset. Singular checks the resulting certificate and native conditions when it consumes a request. Native format alone cannot authorize Insert; otherwise arbitrary non-application datums could claim keys. It need not read the current registry root or promise that Insert will succeed. Singular checks the current key state when applying the operation.

validation-without-mutable-registry-obse.name: docs-certification/validation-without-mutable-registry-observation-02
validation-without-mutable-registry-obse.text: For Update/Delete, the application spending validator approves the operation-specific transfer of the existing NFT. That spending validator must enforce the resulting request's required format, binding and custody in the release transaction. Singular rechecks its native conditions when consuming the request. Establishing the release need not read the mutable registry UTxO.

validation-without-mutable-registry-obse.name: docs-certification/validation-without-mutable-registry-observation-03
validation-without-mutable-registry-obse.text: Authenticated registry configuration may still be needed. The design must bind the registry, request/representative policies, certifier and application destination without circular script-hash dependencies. No concrete configuration layout or hash-cycle solution has been selected.

what-insert-exposes-and-binds.name: docs-certification/what-insert-exposes-and-binds-01
what-insert-exposes-and-binds.text: The logical Insert proposal must expose enough information for certification and the native fold to agree on exactly what will be created:

what-insert-exposes-and-binds.name: docs-certification/what-insert-exposes-and-binds-02
what-insert-exposes-and-binds.text: The registry target, operation, key, initial state and destination must not be substitutable after certification. Native folding verifies that the created NFT output satisfies the certified requirements. These are explicit native output parameters: NFT identity/quantity, destination, datum and value constraints supported by the eventual schema. 'Required effects' is not an unspecified language of arbitrary transaction predicates. Applications needing fresh observations or additional effects at folding fall outside demonstrated precertification coverage unless the native contract explicitly supports them.

what-insert-exposes-and-binds.name: docs-certification/what-insert-exposes-and-binds-03
what-insert-exposes-and-binds.text: The action-token asset name is a hash of a canonical, domain-separated action and its necessary parameters:

what-insert-exposes-and-binds.name: docs-certification/what-insert-exposes-and-binds-04
what-insert-exposes-and-binds.text: The configured application policy approves minting. Singular checks the expected action-bound name. Separate tags prevent treating Insert approval as Withdraw approval. Withdrawal consumes the bound pending Insert without representative minting or a registry update.

what-insert-exposes-and-binds.name: docs-certification/what-insert-exposes-and-binds-05
what-insert-exposes-and-binds.text: Unambiguous canonical encoding and domain separation are required. The specific hash function, binary schema, datum representation, refund economics and token disposal remain open.

which-script-actually-executes.name: docs-certification/which-script-actually-executes-01
which-script-actually-executes.text: Sending an output to a script address does not execute that receiving spending validator. It runs when the output is later consumed. A malformed outsider output can exist at the address without being a valid Singular request. Cardano validation

which-script-actually-executes.name: docs-certification/which-script-actually-executes-02
which-script-actually-executes.text: The division among concrete Singular scripts remains an implementation decision; no extra creation-time request policy is assumed. Recognizing the configured issuer proves where approval came from. It does not prove that an arbitrary application's minting/spending scripts correctly implement their claimed semantics. End-to-end application properties are conditional on those contracts.

which-script-actually-executes.name: docs-certification/which-script-actually-executes-03
which-script-actually-executes.text: If folding has a nonzero net burn under an application action policy, that policy executes in the transaction. A cheap burn branch could avoid repeating expensive semantic checks, but disposal and that branch's contract are still open. Certification can move checks earlier; it does not establish zero application-policy execution or a speedup. Cardano minting policies

which-script-actually-executes.name: docs-certification/which-script-actually-executes-04
which-script-actually-executes.text: The mint field records net quantities per asset, not one ledger action per logical fold operation. If a future construction reuses a representative's asset identity and combines Delete with Insert, their negative/positive quantities could cancel. The fold/request witnesses must still enforce both logical transitions and custody; a mint policy alone cannot be assumed to run when its mint-field entries vanish. This is an inference for Singular's open construction, not a discovered implementation bug. CIP89 discusses net-zero beacon updates and spending-side enforcement. Moving an existing application action token likewise does not rerun its minting policy; token scope and custody must account for that.

recovering-a-registry-command.name: docs-cli-recovery/recovering-a-registry-command-01
recovering-a-registry-command.text: You run singular registry create, open-datum insert, open-datum update, open-datum terminate or inspect (singular registry inspect or open-datum inspect), and something goes wrong between your machine and the chain: the node's answer to a submission never arrives, the process is killed, the machine stops halfway through saving its files, or a transaction the chain had included is rolled back. You want to know which of those happened, you want the next command to pick up from where the last one stopped without sending anything twice, and you want to be told plainly when it cannot.

recovering-a-registry-command.name: docs-cli-recovery/recovering-a-registry-command-02
recovering-a-registry-command.text: This page describes what the ordinary commands do in each case and what you do next. Every write records each transaction it submits in the registry's journal, journal.jsonl, phase by phase, before taking the next step: prepared (the signed body saved beside the journal, before it is sent), the node's answer, the confirmation, and observed (what the transaction made, read back from the chain). A fold's prepared line lists every request it folds, one transition per request, chained from the root before to the root after. The journal is only ever appended to; saved bodies are never rewritten.

the-case-each-submission-met.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-case-each-submission-met-01
the-case-each-submission-met.text: Every write's receipt lists the transactions it prepared under submissions, each with its step, its id, its case and whether its after-state was observed. The case is read from the latest phase the journal holds for the transaction:

the-case-each-submission-met.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-case-each-submission-met-02
the-case-each-submission-met.text: A command that stops after a submission exits partial (status 15), or timeout (13) when the confirmation deadline passed, and its receipt names the case. Nothing is ever sent a second time: a transaction is prepared once, and the journal shows exactly one prepared line for it.

the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-register-keys-00
the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.text: The commands that create a registry and register keys.

the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-register-keys-01
the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.text: As Carol, Alice or Bob running one of the commands of create a registry and register keys on the proved design, you are interrupted in the same ways as above and promised the same thing: the transaction keeps its identity, the next write settles it, and nothing is sent a second time.

the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-register-keys-02
the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.text: Each transaction is journalled as prepared before it is sent, under the step that names it: publish-state-script, publish-application-script and create for open datum's first creation, publish-scripts and create for Singular's, then book, fold, reclaim and cleanup. The journal also records what the first output of the transaction must hold once it is on the chain: a reference script for a publication, the state token for a creation and for a fold, the approval token for a booking, a payment to the refund address for a reclaim and a cleanup. A creation is journalled under the application and the wallet, because the name of the registry it makes is known only once its seed is chosen. The other commands are journalled under the registry and the wallet.

the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-register-keys-03
the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.text: Before it builds anything, the next write of the same wallet reads its journal against the chain. The table shows what it does with an earlier transaction in each case.

the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-register-keys-04
the-commands-that-create-a-registry-and-.text: A transaction the chain does not show cannot be told from one the network has not yet delivered, and these commands never declare it excluded: the next write keeps naming it and stops. Wait for the network and run the command again; a transaction that lands is reconciled. When it can never land, the way out is --state-dir naming another state directory, which starts a fresh journal for that registry and wallet, or for a creation, for that application and wallet; the old journal stays as a record.

the-next-command-reconciles.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-next-command-reconciles-01
the-next-command-reconciles.text: After an inclusion, the command selects its proof state from public state-token history and reads back the step's after-state before appending observed. For a fold of several requests, it reads back every key the fold touches and the registry's state output carrying the last transition's root after. The next ordinary write or inspect reconciles unfinished observations from public chain evidence before proceeding, without submitting anything. Proof state is reconstructed afresh; no mirror or saved-root file is read or written.

the-next-command-reconciles.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-next-command-reconciles-02
the-next-command-reconciles.text: The journal tracks this actor's submissions. It never supplies a replay edge, proof or root. Missing history and a root that does not chain are named refusals; an empty trie cannot substitute for unavailable history. The observation concerns every key the interrupted step touched, even when the current command targets another key: for a fold, every key its transitions name and the registry's state output.

the-next-command-reconciles.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-next-command-reconciles-03
the-next-command-reconciles.text: A write reports reconciliation under reconciled: rolledBack, recovery, excluded and observed. Inspect reports the same fields at the receipt's top level. Inspect reconciles only while no other process holds this directory's write lock; otherwise it reads without reconciling and says so.

the-request-keeps-its-registrys-windows.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-request-keeps-its-registrys-windows-00
the-request-keeps-its-registrys-windows.text: The request keeps its registry's windows.

the-request-keeps-its-registrys-windows.name: docs-cli-recovery/the-request-keeps-its-registrys-windows-01
the-request-keeps-its-registrys-windows.text: As a requester recovering after an interruption, you read processTime and retractTime from registry inspect to see the windows stored in the live state datum. They were chosen once at registry create with --process-time and --retract-time, or defaulted to 600 000 and 300 000 milliseconds (ten and five minutes). Both are fixed for the life of the registry; restarting a command or reconciling its journal does not restart or extend a request's windows. A booking's fold deadline remains its submission time plus the registry's processing window, followed by the owner's retract window.

what-the-checks-show.name: docs-cli-recovery/what-the-checks-show-01
what-the-checks-show.text: The recovery controls run each hosted partition as separate singular processes against its own generated development node, and judge every clause from the receipts the processes printed, the registry's journal, its saved bodies and its files, and — for exclusion and rollback — from the node's own answers, read with devnet probe and its block adoption trace, never through the command under test. The partitions are listed in one place in the root flake; the discovery command prints them for the workflow matrix, and each partition runs by key:

what-the-checks-show.name: docs-cli-recovery/what-the-checks-show-02
what-the-checks-show.text: The combined .#cli-recovery-controls command is retired: it serialised every part on one node and exceeded the receipt cap of 52428800 bytes before reaching never-sent and rollback. The per-partition commands above are generated from the same partition list the workflow matrix uses.

what-the-checks-show.name: docs-cli-recovery/what-the-checks-show-03
what-the-checks-show.text: The rolled-back control is a mechanism of the generated development node — its database restored to an earlier copy — and not a fork of a public chain: it shows what the commands do when the chain they read no longer holds a transaction, not how often or how deeply a public network rolls back. Across every control, each journalled transaction has exactly one prepared line, the journal is only ever appended to, and no saved body changes. These controls do not establish durability across a power loss, only across a killed process.

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures-00
when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: When a bundle waits for signatures.

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures-01
when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: As Bob, I ran a write naming my address and a bundle file, or Alice ran one from her vault, and I want to know where its bundle stands: still waiting for signatures, landed, or dead. The next write in the same state directory tells me, before it builds anything. The bundle's transactions are judged by one thing only: whether the chain holds their identities. Their outputs, their inputs and the after-state of the registry do not count. A transaction of a bundle is its member for its whole life.

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures-02
when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: Pending. Some member is not on chain yet, and the tip has not reached any member's deadline. The next write stops before it builds anything, with status 19, waiting-for-signatures, naming the bundle's hash, its saved path, and the members awaited with their deadlines.

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures-03
when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: Landed. Every member is found on chain. Each gets a landed line with its chain point and confirmations. The next write builds normally, and its receipt reports the bundle under reconciled.

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures-04
when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: Dead. A member can never land. Every member not landed gets a dead line, and the report names the members that went through. The next write builds normally.

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures-05
when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: A bundle dies one of these ways, and the dead line says which:

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures-06
when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: A pending bundle never needs the journal edited. Sign the bundle and send it with singular submit, giving the blueprint of the release the registry was created under with --blueprint because the bundle names a registry (a create bundle needs none), or let a member's deadline pass and run the command again. A vault run whose answer from the node was lost ends partial, and the next write settles its bundle by identity in the same way. A write that sent its transactions and then could not journal the outcome keeps the submission's outcome and its sends in the receipt, and names what failed on its own.

when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures-07
when-a-bundle-waits-for-signatures.text: A bundle sent elsewhere and refused by the node is not seen by your journal, since singular submit keeps no state: it dies when a member's deadline passes. A create bundle has no deadline, so it stays pending. As Alice, if my co-signer never signs the create bundle I staged, or it is refused when sent elsewhere, I correct the cause and send it again. A create from the same wallet without --seed picks the same output again while that output is unspent, so it is stopped at 19 too. The way out is a create that names another output with --seed: a different registry, in a different state directory, which nothing blocks. The pending create's journal stays as a record and blocks nothing else.

when-a-transaction-can-never-land.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-transaction-can-never-land-00
when-a-transaction-can-never-land.text: When a transaction can never land.

when-a-transaction-can-never-land.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-transaction-can-never-land-01
when-a-transaction-can-never-land.text: A transaction carries a validity window. Once the chain's tip has reached the end of that window and an input the transaction spends is still live — so it is not on the chain — it can never be included. The next command appends an excluded line naming the chain point it read and the live inputs. The transaction is settled in the journal: no later command stops on it, and its edge was never applied. A write that excluded a transaction then proceeds, building from the root selected by fresh public replay.

when-a-transaction-can-never-land.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-transaction-can-never-land-02
when-a-transaction-can-never-land.text: What the excluded transaction leaves on chain depends on the command. An excluded update leaves nothing: run it again. The fold of an insert or a terminate is the second of two transactions, and the first, its booking, is on chain: its request stays pending, holding its deposit. Use registry fold while its processing window allows it, registry reclaim with the owner's wallet in its retract window, or registry reject after both windows expire. An insertion's request carries its envelope on chain. A folder reads it publicly and reconstructs proofs from history; neither an insertion fold nor a termination fold needs the booker's files.

when-a-transaction-can-never-land.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-a-transaction-can-never-land-03
when-a-transaction-can-never-land.text: A fold carries an upper bound on its validity window. A booking, and the publications create makes, carry none: a booking that never landed, or one rolled back and not included again, stays unresolved however far the chain moves on, and every write stops on it. That is a known limit of these commands, not a judgement about the transaction.

when-the-chain-rolls-back.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-the-chain-rolls-back-01
when-the-chain-rolls-back.text: A transaction journalled confirmed or observed can leave the chain again. The next command checks every such transaction against the chain it reads: when its first output is not live and an input it spends is live again, it is no longer on the chain, since a transaction on the chain has consumed every input it spends. The command appends a rolled-back line naming the chain point it read and the inputs it found live; for a fold, the line names that its requests are pending again and the public state returns to its root before. The observed line it supersedes stays where it was.

when-the-chain-rolls-back.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-the-chain-rolls-back-02
when-the-chain-rolls-back.text: Proof state follows the public history selected by the current command, including rollbacks. The journal does not rebuild a private trie. The rolled-back transaction is never sent again. If the chain includes it again, the next command journals it confirmed and reconciles its observation; otherwise writes stop on it, naming the case rolled-back.

when-the-next-command-stops.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-the-next-command-stops-01
when-the-next-command-stops.text: A write that finds a transaction it cannot reconcile stops before it builds or submits anything. Its outcome is partial (status 15), and its receipt names the transaction under unresolved with its step, its last journalled phase and its case; the journal does not move.

when-the-next-command-stops.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-the-next-command-stops-02
when-the-next-command-stops.text: acknowledged, unknown or timeout: the chain does not yet show the transaction. Wait for the network and run the command again; when the transaction lands, the next command reconciles it, and when its validity window closes without it, the next command excludes it — for the fold of an insert or a terminate, with the pending request it leaves.

when-the-next-command-stops.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-the-next-command-stops-03
when-the-next-command-stops.text: rolled-back: the chain no longer shows a transaction it had included. Wait and run the command again; it reconciles the transaction if the chain includes it again, and excludes it once its validity window closes without it, with the same pending request when it is a fold. A booking has no window and stays rolled back.

when-the-next-command-stops.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-the-next-command-stops-04
when-the-next-command-stops.text: included: the transaction is on chain, but public history is incomplete or its reconstructed root does not chain. The named trie refusal preserves its existing outcome and exit status; the journal cannot repair public facts.

when-the-next-command-stops.name: docs-cli-recovery/when-the-next-command-stops-05
when-the-next-command-stops.text: inspect names the same unresolved transaction and its case, with the outcome partial, alongside the root and chain point it read.

conformance-api-reference.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/conformance-api-reference-01
conformance-api-reference.text: A contributor changing the conformance library — a story program, a model binding, a comparison, a receipt check, a rendering — wants to click a module and land on its real interface: signatures, documentation, and the highlighted source, for exactly the code this repository ships. This page is the entry point of that reference for the Conformance library: a generated Haddock reference, rebuilt with the documentation site from this same source tree, so what you read here documents exactly the code this candidate was built from. One boundary on that promise is named below: identifiers and modules that belong to other packages are visible in the generated pages but are not clickable, because their documentation is not bundled with this site.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-01
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: The reference cannot drift from the code it claims to document. The site build derives a manifest from the same Conformance source input Haddock ran on: for every module it records the digest of the Haskell source file and the digests of the actual generated module page and source page. The site check then redoes both halves independently from this repository's own source tree — the manifest's module extent must equal the Cabal library extent, each recorded source digest must match the repository's file, and each generated page in the shipped site must match its recorded digest. A reference generated from any other source, however its label reads, fails that comparison; a page edited after generation fails its own digest.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-02
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: Every link inside the generated pages is inspected too. A reference from one module of this library to another — a type, a function, a module, however the tool that generated it spelled it — must resolve to a page of this reference and, where it names an anchor, to an anchor that exists. The check prints how many same-library links it resolved, and this page's links to the generated pages are checked by the site's ordinary link inventory.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-03
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: Dependency documentation is a different matter. The library is built against a JSON, container and text dependency closure, and none of those packages' Haddock pages are bundled into this site: a type such as an aeson value or a strict text appears in the generated pages as a visible label, but it is not a link — following it would leave this site for documentation that is not shipped with it. Neutralizing those labels is decided from the build's own package database, which positively names every module each dependency owns, so a label is only unlinked when it provably belongs to a dependency; a dead or store-path link that reappears fails the site check, and a same-library reference may never be treated as a dependency label to hide a broken link.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-04
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: One further generator class is unlinked by structure. Haddock renders instance method names in each instance's Methods list as same-page links, but emits no matching anchors for them — every instance of a class lists the same method names, so the anchor would have to be duplicated. Those method labels stay visible as plain text inside the instance lists, and the site check both counts them separately and still requires every fragment link outside that exact structure to resolve.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-05
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: The release archive check extends the same discipline to what gets shipped: the staged documentation archive must carry this library's generated reference member for member and byte for byte, alongside the off-chain registry library's, before the ordinary release checks run.

what-the-reference-does-not-claim.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/what-the-reference-does-not-claim-00
what-the-reference-does-not-claim.text: What the reference does not claim.

what-the-reference-does-not-claim.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/what-the-reference-does-not-claim-01
what-the-reference-does-not-claim.text: This reference covers the Conformance library only. The live runner that executes rows against a devnet is an executable, not a library module: its application modules — the run control, the row runners, the wallet, the cage and the observation code — are outside this reference, and the evidence they produce is the published consumer conformance record, not an API claim. Nothing on this page is a publication or release claim — the reference ships with the candidate site and its future archives, and no version is tagged or published by existing here. The behavioral evidence for the library lives in the check commands the documentation records, not in the existence of these pages.

what-this-reference-contains.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/what-this-reference-contains-01
what-this-reference-contains.text: Every module of the Conformance library is listed below. Each entry links two pages of the generated reference: the module page — exports, types, and documented declarations — and the hyperlinked source page with the rendered, highlighted Haskell this candidate was built from. The reference's own full-page index and symbol index are linked here too. On this site the links open the generated pages; read from the repository, the module links open the source files themselves at the revision you are viewing.

what-this-reference-contains.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/what-this-reference-contains-02
what-this-reference-contains.text: The module extent is the public library of the Conformance Cabal file — every exposed module and the one package-internal owner. That complete extent is 31 modules. The 30 exposed modules are what a caller imports: the story programs, the registry rows as programs with their classification, the stories' binding and identity, the ordinary CLI's refusal controls and their receipt-computed verdicts, the model transport and the Lean oracle, the registration and perturbation comparisons, the receipt record and its validation, the refusal attribution, the row inventory, the purpose-unit arithmetic, the node-refusal rendering, the payment observation, the traced replay's classification of a live refusal and the extent of a run's refusals against the model. The one package-internal module, Conformance.Evidence.Asset, owns the asset-movement shape of edge evidence — one movement named by its policy, asset name and quantity, with the JSON encoding that carries those three fields. It is documented here for the contributor reading the facade's implementation; Conformance.Receipt re-exports its type, so no caller import path changes. The extent below is the complete documented module surface, and the site check fails until it and this list agree.

what-this-reference-contains.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/what-this-reference-contains-30
what-this-reference-contains.text: Conformance.RowNames — source — associates historical receipt keys with descriptive requirement names

which-contract-a-story-describes.name: docs-conformance-api-reference/which-contract-a-story-describes-01
which-contract-a-story-describes.text: Conformance.Edge.Permanent describes the first milestone's registration and permanent termination, refusal of the five other encoded registry actions, and refusal of a mixed batch containing an excluded action. Its public requirement remains uncovered until a bounded live consumer comparison receipt establishes it. Compiled refusal tests passing does not assign that product status. Other seven-edge story modules retain the broader contract's descriptions; their historical successes do not establish support in the permanent contract. The consumer record keeps that distinction and the uncovered rows visible.

a-rows-journey-step-by-step.name: docs-conformance-architecture/a-rows-journey-step-by-step-00
a-rows-journey-step-by-step.text: A row's journey, step by step.

a-rows-journey-step-by-step.name: docs-conformance-architecture/a-rows-journey-step-by-step-01
a-rows-journey-step-by-step.text: The expected side and the observed side stay independently derived: the model transport answers from the frozen model, the comparisons read the chain's outputs as the chain paid them, and neither consults the other's assumptions. The rendering then computes every row's state from the receipts that exist — an uncovered row stays uncovered in the published record, and no row's state is typed by hand.

evidence-and-limits.name: docs-conformance-architecture/evidence-and-limits-01
evidence-and-limits.text: This page is a map, not evidence. The executed evidence for the suite is the receipts the runs write and the row states computed from them, published in the consumer conformance record; the reference's freshness is proven by its manifest digests, not by this prose. The structural review this page came from preserved behavior by moving one declaration byte-for-byte with its caller unchanged, and its matched base/head runs are the ticket owner's comparison to read, not a claim made here. The runner's own internal division into owners remains deferred to the conformance epic's owner after the active semantic work lands; this page does not claim it delivered. No local build, test or documentation run backs this page's claims — the exact-head CI of the candidate that carries it is the verifier, and until that evidence exists these are design statements, not verified facts.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-conformance-architecture/the-story-this-serves-00
the-story-this-serves.text: The story this serves.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-conformance-architecture/the-story-this-serves-01
the-story-this-serves.text: As a contributor, I add or change a conformance row's program, its model binding or its comparison in one focused module, and the executed cases, receipts and published evidence stay exactly what they were — so a reviewer asks one question, and the public record a consuming project reads does not move under them.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-conformance-architecture/the-story-this-serves-02
the-story-this-serves.text: As an integrator reading the consumer conformance record, I need the suite's own structure to keep its promise: rows become executed only through receipts, uncovered rows stay published, and the description language says what each case asserts — whatever module a change lands in.

what-may-not-change.name: docs-conformance-architecture/what-may-not-change-01
what-may-not-change.text: These are the suite's public promises, and a structural change that breaks one of them is not an improvement:

what-may-not-change.name: docs-conformance-architecture/what-may-not-change-02
what-may-not-change.text: A row becomes executed only through a receipt written by a run that actually executed it; row states are computed from receipts and never typed.

what-may-not-change.name: docs-conformance-architecture/what-may-not-change-03
what-may-not-change.text: Uncovered rows are published, not hidden; a green step is never presented as a fulfilled consumer promise.

what-may-not-change.name: docs-conformance-architecture/what-may-not-change-04
what-may-not-change.text: Every product claim is expressed in the suite's description language, and execution and rendering of that language are total over the same instruction set.

what-may-not-change.name: docs-conformance-architecture/what-may-not-change-05
what-may-not-change.text: Surfaces a reader navigates carry requirement text, not internal identifiers; harness evidence stays in its marked appendix.

what-may-not-change.name: docs-conformance-architecture/what-may-not-change-06
what-may-not-change.text: No case predicate, expected outcome, verdict classification, instruction, receipt field, theorem binding or evidence claim moves by a restructure.

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-conformance-architecture/which-way-dependencies-run-01
which-way-dependencies-run.text: The library never imports the app: the arrow runs one way, from the live runner into the library. The app modules — the command router and the row runners, the wallet, cage and submission owners, and Conformance.Run.Live, the interpreter that gives the story programs their live effects — are executables, outside the generated reference and documented here only by their boundary. The runner's own internal division is deferred work owned by the conformance epic, not delivered by the review this page came from; what this map promises is the library side of that boundary.

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-conformance-architecture/which-way-dependencies-run-02
which-way-dependencies-run.text: One owner inside the evidence group is new and deliberately small: Conformance.Evidence.Asset owns the asset-movement shape of edge evidence — one movement named by its policy, asset name and quantity, with the JSON encoding that carries those three fields. It used to be the last declaration of Conformance.Receipt that is not a receipt concern. Conformance.Receipt re-exports it unchanged, so the one real caller, the live runner's keyed-mint expectation and observation, imports it through exactly the path it used before; the runner is not edited by that move.

who-owns-the-conformance-suite.name: docs-conformance-architecture/who-owns-the-conformance-suite-01
who-owns-the-conformance-suite.text: Dated qualification, 2026-10-15: rejection after the window, rejection before the deadline, request value and refund routing, rejection and retraction refund controls, and rejection inside the processing and retraction windows are all unmet by ruling: implementation follows the superseded rule; the ruled rule is not implemented. The live comparisons still exercise the legacy rejection that spends the registry state output. The ruled rejection reads that output by reference and never spends it. Agreement with the legacy path is not acceptance of the ruled design. The earlier processing-window consumer requirement and the unresolved refund-routing requirement remain open. Historical results below retain their original revision and evidence binding; they do not establish current acceptance.

who-owns-the-conformance-suite.name: docs-conformance-architecture/who-owns-the-conformance-suite-02
who-owns-the-conformance-suite.text: A contributor changing the conformance suite — adding a row's story, re-binding a theorem, adjusting a comparison, tightening the receipt record, re-rendering the published evidence — wants to open the one module that owns that concern and know which way the dependencies run, before touching a two-thousand-line live interpreter. This page is that map for the suite's library: what each concern's owner is, where the live runner's boundary sits, what may never change while the code moves, where to make a common change, and what the evidence does and does not show. The library's generated interface is the Conformance API reference; this page explains the responsibilities behind it.

appendix-checking-the-published-comparis.name: docs-consumer-conformance/appendix-checking-the-published-comparisons-01
appendix-checking-the-published-comparis.text: The appendix loads the actual requirement inventory, discovers every holding journey statement, and checks its previous-design outcome, model declaration binding, uncovered classification without comparison receipts, and stated evidence boundary. It also checks that the reader renders each requirement's text. These publication checks establish no application-held model comparison.

appendix-how-the-statements-are-checked.name: docs-consumer-conformance/appendix-how-the-statements-are-checked-00
appendix-how-the-statements-are-checked.text: Appendix: how the statements are checked.

appendix-how-the-statements-are-checked.name: docs-consumer-conformance/appendix-how-the-statements-are-checked-01
appendix-how-the-statements-are-checked.text: This appendix is harness evidence and says nothing more about the product. The hosted conformance checks list the inventory with the runner, then require of every row in the group that it reads uncovered, gives its reason, states the previous design's outcome, names its declarations and both hosted jobs, retypes no number and names no internal identifier, and that the five early-rejection rows are unchanged. The same script then runs thirteen times against scratch copies with one wrong fact planted each, and must refuse every one.

consumer-conformance-record.name: docs-consumer-conformance/consumer-conformance-record-01
consumer-conformance-record.text: Dated qualification, 2026-10-15: rejection after the window, rejection before the deadline, request value and refund routing, rejection and retraction refund controls, and rejection inside the processing and retraction windows are all unmet by ruling: implementation follows the superseded rule; the ruled rule is not implemented.
