consumer-and-ledger-boundary.text: The historical Cage types establish encodings and precedents. KERI pre-rotation commits to key digests; naming recovery commits to a complete canonical address.

evidence-and-release-status.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/evidence-and-release-status-01
evidence-and-release-status.text: The lifecycle panel inspects maintenance, recovery and both termination routes, including their computed refusal reasons. The downloadable archive binds model, scenarios, replay code, toolchain inputs and identity ledgers with a SHA-256 manifest. Candidate results distinguish the registry's compiled and connected CLI checks from these naming design observations.

evidence-and-release-status.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/evidence-and-release-status-02
evidence-and-release-status.text: Lean proofs, finite model replay, inspected lifecycle rows, a built archive and a live preview do not establish a deployed naming validator or downstream consumer acceptance. Uncovered consumer requirements remain visible.

how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry-00
how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.text: How a name moves in the registry.

how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry-01
how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.text: A name is one key in the registry's authenticated map. Registration changes an unknown key to Active and delivers an active witness to its bound destination. Termination burns that witness and changes the key to Terminal permanently. The legacy Absent byte remains a raw encoding for invalid-context controls; registration cannot create it. The five excluded operations are refused.

how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry-02
how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.text: The current registry contract has a fixed compiled admission boundary. Naming certifies each supported edge in advance by minting an approval binding the edge, key, owner and destination. The registry recomputes that binding. Folding is permissionless; approval prevents the folder from substituting another destination. Naming's separate application validator governs maintenance, recovery and authorization to retire.

recover-with-the-committed-next-controll.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/recover-with-the-committed-next-controller-00
recover-with-the-committed-next-controll.text: Recover with the committed next controller.

recover-with-the-committed-next-controll.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/recover-with-the-committed-next-controller-01
recover-with-the-committed-next-controll.text: Recovery reveals the complete next controller address, verifies its stored commitment and requires its payment-key signer. The current controller need not sign. The successor retains the active witness, installs the revealed controller and stores a fresh next commitment. The consumed commitment cannot be replayed.

recover-with-the-committed-next-controll.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/recover-with-the-committed-next-controller-02
recover-with-the-committed-next-controll.text: The commitment is BLAKE2b-256("singular/naming/next-control/v1" || 0x00 || canonical-address-bytes). It covers the complete binary Cardano address, including header and network. Canonical base and enterprise addresses with payment-key credentials are supported; script payment credentials cannot authorize recovery. Wrong-domain, wrong-address and wrong-payment-key controls accompany the positive vectors.

refused-historical-encodings.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/refused-historical-encodings-01
refused-historical-encodings.text: The wire format retains insertAbsent, updateActive, deleteAbsent, deleteActive and witnessTerminal with their original tags. The current compiled registry refuses all five, including mixed batches and caller-constructed contexts. The archived broader design preserves earlier absence, deletion and witnessing stories; they are not current supported operations.

retire-permanently.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/retire-permanently-01
retire-permanently.text: Termination needs the committed recovery key or a distinct-member retirement quorum. The current control key alone cannot authorize it. This preserves the holder's recovery remedy if the everyday key is stolen.

retire-permanently.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/retire-permanently-02
retire-permanently.text: Authorization moves the active witness into completion-only application custody, mints a bound terminating approval and creates the completion request. Anyone may fold that request: the application custody is spent, the witness is burned and the key becomes Terminal. This completion custody is distinct from the removed registry Absent-custody implementation.

retire-permanently.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/retire-permanently-03
retire-permanently.text: Terminal witnessing is refused by this contract. A terminal name has no remaining supported transition. Retirement prevents name-based resolution but cannot retract a raw address someone already saved.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/who-this-is-for-00
who-this-is-for.text: Who this is for.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/who-this-is-for-01
who-this-is-for.text: A name holder wants to change where a live name receives payments, recover after losing the current control key, or end the name permanently. A new participant can register an unknown name. Registry transitions are registration and permanent termination; application maintenance and recovery preserve the registry root.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-naming-lifecycle/who-this-is-for-02
who-this-is-for.text: Open the simulator and select Naming — permanent retirement. Its lifecycle panel inspects the rows computed by Lean. This is design-time evidence, not an observed ledger execution.

a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update.name: docs-negative-host/a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update-00
a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update.text: A closed registry refuses an update.

a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update.name: docs-negative-host/a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update-01
a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update.text: Some registries are closed: created with open-datum create --closed, their payloads are written once, and no update ever lands. The ordinary client says so before it builds anything — an update on a closed registry is refused on the machine, with nothing submitted. The host skips the client and asks the chain instead.

a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update.name: docs-negative-host/a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update-02
a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update.text: Alice registers alice-1 in a closed registry and folds it active, both with the ordinary commands. Through the host she then submits her own honest update of that key, signed by her, with no tamper flag and no local evaluation. The node refuses it, and the verdict names the registry's own closed application in the spending role: the refusal comes from the chain's script, not from the client's policy. A fresh read shows the registry exactly as it was. The create receipt names the closed application, and its pin is the closed pin — it matches the closed preview's pin and differs from the open pin of the same seed, so the refused script can only be closed-datum's.

a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update.name: docs-negative-host/a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update-03
a-closed-registry-refuses-an-update.text: The control runs in the same registry, on the same key: Alice books its termination and folds it, with the ordinary commands. The node accepts both, and the key reads as terminal. The chain refuses the update and nothing else.

a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-an.name: docs-negative-host/a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-and-its-owner-reclaims-it-00
a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-an.text: A refused insertion strands a booking, and its owner reclaims it.

a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-an.name: docs-negative-host/a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-and-its-owner-reclaims-it-01
a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-an.text: An insertion of a taken key is refused at its fold, not at its booking, so the booking the host made stays pending on the chain, holding its deposit. The owner takes it back with the ordinary command:

a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-an.name: docs-negative-host/a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-and-its-owner-reclaims-it-02
a-refused-insertion-strands-a-booking-an.text: The reclaim is governed by time, and the timing matters. A booking's retract window opens only after the registry's processing window has passed — that ordering is the model's own, not a client convenience — so a reclaim submitted earlier is refused by the ordinary command before signing: it reports not-phase2 and submits nothing. The scenario run creates its registry with a processing window of 120 seconds and a retract window of 600 seconds (the other scenarios use a 30-second retract window), then waits out the two minutes of processing before submitting one reclaim. This is a timed reclaim, not an immediate one. The reclaim's receipt names the command (reclaim), its outcome (success), the request and its edge (insertActive), and the read afterwards shows the booking collected and the deposit returned to its owner.

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-00
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: Every forbidden move, and what refuses it.

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-01
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: The scenario set is fourteen pairs in ten stories: the rewrite of a protected field has five variants, one per protected field. Each pair is one forbidden command and its accepting control, run on a fresh development node from the extracted release archive. The pair list itself lives in applications/open-datum/negative/pairs.json; the model statements behind the thirteen open-registry refusals are on the ticket's data model page. The write-once rule behind closed-update has no Lean statement, by operator ruling: the closed registry's refusal is shown by the run, not by a theorem.

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-02
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: After the command-line split landed (lambdasistemi/singular#528), the ordinary surface is two executables: singular, with the registry's own commands — create, fold, reject, reclaim, inspect — and open-datum, with the application's — insert, update, terminate, fold, inspect. The host keeps one namespace, singular-negative registry …, with the shared flag group, so a host command reads the same today as it did before the split. The mirrors named below are the post-split ordinary spellings.

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-03
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: Read the four insertion rows together, because their timing is the subtle part: an insertion is only a request. Under the host, the booking of a taken key is accepted — a request is a request — and the refusal comes later, when the host folds it and the registry's state validator sees the key is already held. The ordinary client stops the same move much earlier, from its own reading of the registry's entry, which is exactly why the host exists: only it can show you the chain's own answer.

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-04
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: Three forms have no ordinary equivalent at all, and they are the host's own spellings:

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-05
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: registry withdraw spends a holding directly, with the release redeemer, outside any fold. The ordinary surface has no such command: a release exists only inside the fold of a booked termination.

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-06
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: registry update … --tamper FIELD rewrites one protected field of the holding's record — controller, deposit, token, address or datum. The ordinary update accepts no such flag and cannot express the move.

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-07
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: registry fold … --pay-short N builds the fold paying the controller that many lovelace less than owed. The ordinary fold has no flag to deviate from what is owed.

every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.name: docs-negative-host/every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it-08
every-forbidden-move-and-what-refuses-it.text: Every ordinary spelling the host accepts is handed to the shared parser unchanged, and the ordinary executables refuse these three bypass spellings as unknown commands — the release check reads the built ordinary executables to prove they contain no host module and no copy of the bypass.

how-to-run-it.name: docs-negative-host/how-to-run-it-01
how-to-run-it.text: From a checkout of this repository — the command assembles the release archive itself, extracts it outside the checkout, and builds the host, the ordinary executables and the development node from the archive's own flakes:

how-to-run-it.name: docs-negative-host/how-to-run-it-02
how-to-run-it.text: One scenario run starts a fresh node, funds Alice and Bob, runs the forbidden command and its accepting control, judges every clause from the receipts alone, and scans every receipt and output for the key bytes the run generated (keys are given by path and never printed). The fourteen scenario names are the pairs of the table above.

how-to-run-it.name: docs-negative-host/how-to-run-it-03
how-to-run-it.text: The hosted workflow runs every pair on every push: it discovers the scenario list from the host's own table, runs each scenario as its own job from the release archive, and aggregates them under the two stable check names Negative host pairs and Negative host mutants. Those two names are what a repository can require; the jobs beneath them may grow as pairs are added, the names stay.

the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination.name: docs-negative-host/the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination-00
the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination.text: The short fold of a booked termination.

the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination.name: docs-negative-host/the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination-01
the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination.text: One sequence carries the most rules at once, over one request. Alice has registered alice-2 and is its controller. She books its termination and stops at the pending request; the termination is not done until a fold settles it. Bob, who is nobody in particular, then tries to settle it for less than owed, and finally settles it honestly.

the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination.name: docs-negative-host/the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination-02
the-short-fold-of-a-booked-termination.text: The sequence is connected over one pending request. Alice, the controller of alice-2, books its termination with the ordinary command and stops at the pending request; the termination is not done until a fold settles it. Bob, who is nobody in particular, first settles it for one lovelace less than owed, through the host: the application's script at the fold refuses, the request stays pending, the deposit stays held. Bob then folds the same request honestly, through the same host and from the same state: the honest fold burns the key's token, leaves the key terminal and pays the controller exactly what the booking owes. The one difference between the two folds is the payment, and that difference alone moves the verdict from refusal to acceptance.

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-00
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: What a run does not show.

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-01
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: A refusal shows the rule held for that transaction on that chain; the model statements and validator tests carry the general guarantee. The runs on this page are evidence about each transaction they ran, not a proof about every transaction there could be.

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-02
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: What is deliberately not there yet:

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-03
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: Rejection pairs. A folder turning a request away is not among the pairs; protected rejection is its own work (lambdasistemi/singular#498, lambdasistemi/singular#529).

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-04
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: Two update rules with no pair. The rule that a continuation keeps at least the protected deposit in its value, and the rule that exactly one output carries the key's token, are refused earlier by other rules in every pair here, so neither is exercised by its own pair (lambdasistemi/singular#552).

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-05
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: Each pair must be able to fail. A green refusal proves nothing unless a validator that dropped the rule would have accepted the move. For every refusing rule a mutant validator removes exactly that rule, the release archive is rebuilt from the mutated source, and the pair must flip — the node must accept what the rule refuses. Nine mutants cover all fourteen pairs.

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-06
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: The crafting exists twice. The conformance harness keeps its own copy of the crafted transactions; the host's copy is the one the release archive ships (lambdasistemi/singular#551).

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-07
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: A finished local run may leave its node behind. A part run locally can leave its development node and working directories on the machine (lambdasistemi/singular#560); hosted runners are unaffected.

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-08
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: The registry row removes two things at once because one alone could never flip: taking out only the labelled refusal leaves the node refusing, since the insert step makes the same check itself. The runner builds this mutant the same way as the others, inside its own scratch copy only: the pin of the registry's state script, the registry manifest, the permanent-contract file and the known-scripts module are regenerated, and so are the application's blueprint, manifest and record, so the executables built there accept the mutated hashes. The checkout, the shipped loader and the permanent contract are not changed, and the run checks that. The control pair for this mutant is stranger-updates-the-key.

what-a-run-does-not-show.name: docs-negative-host/what-a-run-does-not-show-09
what-a-run-does-not-show.text: The mutant table is the honest measure of the refusal evidence: each row names the one rule a validator had to lose before the chain would take the move it refuses today. Beside every mutant a control pair that a different rule refuses must stay refused, so a patch that disabled more than its named rule could not hide.

what-each-command-prints.name: docs-negative-host/what-each-command-prints-01
what-each-command-prints.text: Each host command prints one JSON receipt on standard output. For a refused move it carries: the command and its outcome class (ledger-refusal — distinct from client-refusal, encoding-failure and setup-failure, which are never counted as the chain's word), the node's own refusal text, the failed script hashes with their roles in the opened registry, the registry's application and state pins, and two reads — before and after — of the registry state root, the key's holding with its value and envelope, the wallet's outputs, the pending requests and the held deposit. A pair passes only when the after-read equals the before-read.

what-each-command-prints.name: docs-negative-host/what-each-command-prints-02
what-each-command-prints.text: For an accepted command the receipt names what the chain took: the update names its transaction id, a booking names the request it created, a fold names the requests it folded. So one run shows both halves: the transaction the host really built, and the node's own verdict on it.

what-singular-negative-shows.name: docs-negative-host/what-singular-negative-shows-01
what-singular-negative-shows.text: You are evaluating Singular, and this repository is all you have. It claims rules: only a key's controller may update that key, a key the registry already holds cannot be taken again, a holding is released only inside a fold. This page shows where those rules are enforced — on the chain, by scripts — and how you can watch each refusal happen from the release archive, with no trust in the client that ships with the repository.

who-refuses-what.name: docs-negative-host/who-refuses-what-01
who-refuses-what.text: One move, two clients. The ordinary client answers from its own local policy; the negative host sends the move to the node and the chain's scripts answer.

who-refuses-what.name: docs-negative-host/who-refuses-what-02
who-refuses-what.text: The diagram follows one move through the two clients. The ordinary client answers from its own reading of the key's envelope — it names a controller, and this signer is not it — and submits nothing. The negative host builds the transaction, signs with whatever key file was named, submits with no local check and no local script evaluation, and the chain's scripts answer: the application's spending contract for a spend of a holding, the registry's state validator for a fold. The refusal comes back with the failing script's hash and its role in the registry the command opened — application-spending, application-at-fold or state-validator — and a fresh read confirms nothing moved. Nothing is typed in: the expected script is read from the registry's own pins, so a pass never comes from a literal someone wrote down.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-00
who-this-is-for.text: Who this is for.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-01
who-this-is-for.text: You are a person deciding whether to build on Singular. The ordinary client is polite to its user: several of the registry's rules it enforces itself, before your transaction ever leaves the machine. A refusal from the client proves nothing about the chain, so politeness is exactly what an evaluator must be able to switch off.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-02
who-this-is-for.text: singular-negative is that switch. It is its own executable in the release archive, built from the same command-line and registry sources as the ordinary executables, with the safeguards taken out: it builds the transaction you asked for, signs with whatever key file you name, skips every local check and every local script evaluation, and submits. The node takes the transaction or refuses it, and when it refuses, the verdict names the script that refused.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-03
who-this-is-for.text: Two people make it concrete. Alice has registered the key alice-1 and is its controller; Bob is anyone else. Bob types the same move to both executables.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-04
who-this-is-for.text: To the ordinary client:

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-05
who-this-is-for.text: The client reads the key's envelope, sees that its controller is not the key that would sign, and refuses: the envelope's controller is 0x… but this command signs as 0x…. Nothing is submitted. The node never sees the move.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-06
who-this-is-for.text: To the negative host, the same move:

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-07
who-this-is-for.text: Both executables read new.json the same way: ordinary JSON is stored as plain JSON, and a file in the detailed schema is given with --payload-schema detailed, as store ordinary JSON as a key's payload says.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-08
who-this-is-for.text: The negative host's parts keep key files as harness controls: it signs with whatever key file you name and opens no vault, so its command lines on this page name --wallet-skey, and only they do. Every open-datum line a reader types here signs from a vault (--vault FILE, the passphrase typed once at the prompt, or read from --passphrase-fd N in a script) or names an address and a bundle file for a signer elsewhere.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-09
who-this-is-for.text: The host builds the update, signs it as Bob, and submits it unevaluated. The application's spending contract refuses it, the node's verdict names that script, and a fresh read shows the registry, the key's holding and the wallets exactly as they were.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-negative-host/who-this-is-for-10
who-this-is-for.text: Beside every forbidden move its accepting control runs too: the same command with the one forbidden difference removed, from the same registry state, signed by the same signer. A refusal only means something when the same machinery succeeds on the next line.

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-00
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: A worked example: resolving a registry before showing it.

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-01
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: As a third-party reader built on this library, I am handed the address of a registry and want to show what it holds. A registry's datum pins four policies, and a genuine registry can pin policies its creator chose, so what I read from the datum means nothing until I have compared the pins with the ones the application derives. Singular.Registry.StateToken.resolveRegistry is that comparison. It takes the application, the release the registry was created under, the state token and one view of the chain, and gives back either the registry, whose datum has passed every check, or the refusal that names the first thing that does not.

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-02
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: Over Mallory's registry, whose datum pins an active policy of her own, the function never reaches the first branch and the program prints:

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-03
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: The application you pass decides which pins are compared. An application that knows its own script, whether it states it as a blueprint title applied to the registry, as a compiled script or as a hash, has its application policy compared as well as the active witness policy. The neutral value used above knows none, so it takes the application policy from the datum, compares the active policy, and records that in the resolved registry: resolvedApplicationPin says whether the application policy was compared or was not checked against any blueprint, and a reader that shows registry content says so. A program that derives several applications from one registry, as open-datum does for its open and its closed registries, calls resolveRegistryAmong with its candidates and gets back the registry and the candidate the datum's application policy selects. pinsDifference is the comparison itself, exported for a command that creates a registry and wants to compare the datum it reads back with the pins it built.

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-04
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: The comparison is made when the registry is resolved and not again within the same run, because every fold preserves the pinned policies on chain; the protocol page says why a reader must make it.

appendix-discovered-adapter-consumers.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/appendix-discovered-adapter-consumers-01
appendix-discovered-adapter-consumers.text: This source inventory explains ownership, not ledger coverage. Each retained owner below uses serial access for the stated lifetime. Test producers stay independent of the pure computation being compared. No public interface or retained journey is removed.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-01
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: The reference cannot drift from the code it claims to document. The site build derives a manifest from the same off-chain source input Haddock ran on: for every module it records the digest of the Haskell source file and the digest of the actual generated source page. The site check then redoes both halves independently from this repository's own source tree — the manifest's module extent must equal the Cabal library extent, each recorded source digest must match the repository's file, and each generated page in the shipped site must match its recorded digest. A reference generated from any other source, however its label reads, fails that comparison; a page edited after generation fails its own digest.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-02
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: Every link inside the generated pages is inspected too. A reference from one module of this library to another — a type, a function, a module, however the tool that generated it spelled it — must resolve to a page of this reference and, where it names an anchor, to an anchor that exists. The check prints how many same-library links it resolved, and the reference's own index and guide links are checked by the site's ordinary link inventory.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-03
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: Dependency documentation is a different matter. The library is built against a large Cardano and Plutus dependency closure, and none of those packages' Haddock pages are bundled into this site: a type such as a ledger address or a Plutus core data value appears in the generated pages as a visible label, but it is not a link — following it would leave this site for documentation that is not shipped with it. Neutralizing those labels is decided from the build's own package database, which positively names every module each dependency owns, so a label is only unlinked when it provably belongs to a dependency; a dead or store-path link that reappears fails the site check, and a same-library reference may never be treated as a dependency label to hide a broken link.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-04
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: One further generator class is unlinked by structure. Haddock renders instance method names in each instance's Methods list as same-page links, but emits no matching anchors for them — every instance of a class lists the same method names, so the anchor would have to be duplicated. Those method labels stay visible as plain text inside the instance lists, and the site check both counts them separately and still requires every fragment link outside that exact structure to resolve.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-05
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: The release archive check extends the same discipline to what gets shipped: the staged documentation archive must carry the generated reference member for member and byte for byte before the ordinary release checks run.

interruptible-confirmation.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/interruptible-confirmation-01
interruptible-confirmation.text: An application author supplying registry capabilities wants a cancelled or expired command to stop its confirmation wait while retaining the transaction it already submitted. Registry commands and open-datum writes call capConfirm on the command's calling thread under the confirmation deadline. The callback confirms exactly the supplied signed transaction; it does not submit it again or start a background confirmation worker.

interruptible-confirmation.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/interruptible-confirmation-02
interruptible-confirmation.text: The command owns the wait and its cleanup. An IO callback must be interruptible through its transport reads, polling and resource cleanup, and must propagate asynchronous exceptions. A replacement that holds an uninterruptible block delays both deadline return and caller cancellation until that block releases. That is a capability limitation: it does not create a worker that can escape the command. Test harnesses observing this limit must release their barrier and join their command.

interruptible-confirmation.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/interruptible-confirmation-03
interruptible-confirmation.text: After acceptance by the submission endpoint, confirmation failure or deadline expiry leaves the signed identity journalled as unconfirmed. Caller cancellation also preserves that unresolved identity before propagating the original interruption. A provider failure is partial evidence, a deadline is a timeout, and neither is a ledger refusal or permission to resubmit. Success records confirmation; the command's independent readback remains a later step. The final receipt boundary rethrows asynchronous interruptions and a concrete WaitFailure unchanged: an infrastructure wait failure supplies no verdict and does not become a client or ledger refusal. Ordinary synchronous command failures and fallback receipts retain their existing classification. The module and field contract are in Singular.Registry.Capabilities. This effect contract leaves Lean's transaction law and the public capability signature unchanged.

off-chain-api-reference.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/off-chain-api-reference-01
off-chain-api-reference.text: A contributor reading the builder and blueprint guide wants to click a module of this library and land on its real interface — signatures, documentation, and the highlighted source — for exactly the code this repository ships. This page is the entry point of that reference for the off-chain registry library: a generated Haddock reference, rebuilt with the documentation site from this same source tree, so what you read here documents exactly the code this candidate was built from — and, as the extent below states, a few of its modules are documented for the contributor without being importable by a caller. One boundary on that promise is named below: identifiers and modules that belong to other packages are visible in the generated pages but are not clickable, because their documentation is not bundled with this site.

snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compatibility-01
snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.text: As a library consumer, you can compute a root, membership or exclusion proof, or an authenticated leaf from an MPF database value without allocating a mutable manager. The computation uses the existing MPF core and never treats the uncommitted key index as evidence for a leaf. A foreign observed root refuses authentication; inconsistent nodes prove no leaf. Malformed node decoding can still raise an exception, so the caller owns its evaluation and exception boundary.

snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compatibility-02
snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.text: The legacy names mkPureTrie, mkPureTrieFromRef, mkPureTrieManager and mkPureTrieManagerFrom identify the in-memory backend. Their IO adapters remain mutable. A caller owns the adapter and any dump action for the entire serial builder, replay or mirror lifetime. There is no locking or thread-safety guarantee. Sharing requires external serialization of complete sessions, including reads, writes, speculative snapshots, visibility changes and dumps. A dump includes hidden tries and is not an atomic concurrent snapshot. Missing and hidden manager lookups retain their existing exceptions, Trie not found: and Trie is hidden: followed by the shown token. Speculative sessions execute the existing pure stateTrie over a snapshot and discard the resulting database, without allocating a mutable copy. Action and mutation failures still occur during the IO callback; the returned value stays lazy, as it did with the mutable callback.

snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compatibility-03
snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.text: Ordinary registry and open-datum commands already authenticate through TrieState; the direct executable callers of the older CLI.Proof snapshot functions are the preservation tests. Removing their allocation alone is therefore a library computation improvement, not a claim that command session ownership changed.

what-the-reference-does-not-claim.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/what-the-reference-does-not-claim-00
what-the-reference-does-not-claim.text: What the reference does not claim.

what-the-reference-does-not-claim.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/what-the-reference-does-not-claim-01
what-the-reference-does-not-claim.text: This reference covers the off-chain registry library only. The four registry commands — the journey, insert-active, update-terminal and deployment — are executables, not library modules: their command-local modules are documented with source links in Who owns a registry command, and the library interfaces they call are the ones listed above. The conformance suite's own library now has its own generated reference — the Conformance API reference — generated and checked by the same discipline from the Conformance tree. Together the two references cover the documented module surfaces of the two public libraries, no more: this reference's extent is the off-chain main library's, with the runtime service modules staying outside it in Runtime service ownership, and the conformance reference's extent is the conformance library's. The executables and the on-chain Aiken validators remain outside the generated references. The public local-services component also exposes LocalEvaluation, NetworkTime, ProviderSettings, ProviderTrace, SessionEvidence, SessionIO, SessionServices, TimeMaterial, TimeSource, Trace, TraceRender, WaitTypes and Wallet; their sources live under offchain/local-services/Singular/Registry/. Their generated pages are not in this main-library reference. The public open-datum-application component (applications/open-datum/offchain/) carries the open-datum application the command line composes — entry commands, envelope, booking approval and destination, payload update, release rules, script, and the application value — and the request builders of the registry on the proved design: the booking of a registration, its reclaim by the refund address and its cleanup after the window, the configuration record added to the creation of a registry, the records and actions of the request validator in the layout it decodes, the validator as a transaction carries it, the reasons a builder declines, what open datum hands the fold of a registry, and the commands that create a registry and book, reclaim and clean up a registration: Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Book, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Build, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Command, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Entry, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Envelope, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.InsertEnvelope, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Permanent, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Plan, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Preview, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Registration, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Release, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Booking, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Configuration, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Fold, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Pending, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Records, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Refusal, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Script, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Root, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Run, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Script, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Update and Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Value; their sources live under applications/open-datum/offchain/src/Singular/Application/OpenDatum/, and the executable's entry point lives in applications/open-datum/offchain/app/. The public registry-cli component (offchain/cli/) carries the registry command line the two binaries link — session, journal and receipts, the flag group, create, fold, reject, reclaim, inspect, reconcile, recovery, the booking call and the creation of a registry on the proved design with the fold into it: Singular.CLI, Singular.CLI.Attached, Singular.CLI.Command, Singular.CLI.Create, Singular.CLI.Finish, Singular.CLI.Fold, Singular.CLI.FoldRules, Singular.CLI.Inspect, Singular.CLI.Key, Singular.CLI.Live, Singular.CLI.ManagedState, Singular.CLI.Outlay, Singular.CLI.Payload, Singular.CLI.Permanent, Singular.CLI.Plan, Singular.CLI.Promise, Singular.CLI.Proof, Singular.CLI.Receipt, Singular.CLI.ReceiptBody, Singular.CLI.Reclaim, Singular.CLI.ReclaimRules, Singular.CLI.Reconcile, Singular.CLI.Recovery, Singular.CLI.Registry, Singular.CLI.Reject, Singular.CLI.RejectRules, Singular.CLI.RequestWindow, Singular.CLI.Root, Singular.CLI.Session, Singular.CLI.State, Singular.CLI.Steps, Singular.CLI.Trace, Singular.CLI.TrieHistory and Singular.CLI.TrieTrace; their sources live under offchain/cli/src/Singular/CLI/.

what-the-reference-does-not-claim.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/what-the-reference-does-not-claim-02
what-the-reference-does-not-claim.text: The registry packages export the booking check every ordinary verb runs before signing: bookingRefusal in Singular.CLI.Booking decides, from the key's current entry, whether the entry rules out the booking, naming the key, the verb, and the leaves found and required. Every ordinary verb of an application calls it in planning, in preview and live, so a taken key, a terminal key, and an unknown key for update and terminate are refused before any signing key is read. A cardano-keri application gets the same refusal by calling the exported function in its own planning. The negative host lives beside the application in applications/open-datum/negative/, with its sources under applications/open-datum/negative/src/Negative/ and its entry point in applications/open-datum/negative/app/. Their generated pages are not in this main-library reference either: only the main library has a generated reference. This coverage gap stays visible; wider generated coverage is a separate decision for the epic's owner, not a claim this page makes. Nothing on this page is a publication or release claim — the reference ships with the candidate site and its future archives, and no version is tagged or published by existing here. The behavioral evidence for the moved builder, blueprint and wire code lives in the check commands the off-chain development guide records, not in the existence of these pages.

what-this-reference-contains.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/what-this-reference-contains-02
what-this-reference-contains.text: The module extent is the public library of the off-chain Cabal file — every exposed module, every internal module, and every module the library re-exports under its own name. That complete extent is 77 modules in three kinds: 60 explicitly exposed modules and 4 re-exported modules are what a caller imports; the two trie capability owners behind the TrieState facade (Singular.Registry.TrieState.Core and .Types), the three fold owners behind the Update facade — Singular.Registry.TxBuilder.Update.Build, .Context and .Duties — the five wire owners behind the Types facade — Singular.Registry.Wire.Primitive, .Request, .State, .Proof and .Redeemer — and the three deployment owners behind the Deployment facade — Singular.Registry.Deployment.Manifest, .Mirror and .Attach — are package-internal other-modules with generated pages here for the contributor reading the facades' implementations, but no caller import path: a caller compiles against the facades' exports, not against these modules. Singular.Registry.Ledger, Singular.Registry.LedgerProvider, Singular.Registry.Evidence and Singular.Registry.Signing are the re-exports: their implementations are owned by the public local-services component (offchain/local-services/) and the main library exposes their stable import paths. The generic provider interface and evidence types let a caller supply capabilities without selecting a node runtime; the Koios constructor supplies unbound, unverified HTTP facts through that interface. The runtime service modules outside this extent — the terminal composition and its transport in koios-http, and the remaining service modules of local-services — are documented with source links in Runtime service ownership. The extent below is the complete documented module surface — exposed, re-exported and package-internal alike; the site check fails until it and this list agree.
