what-this-reference-contains.text: Test support, documented because it is public to the test modules:

evidence-and-limits.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/evidence-and-limits-01
evidence-and-limits.text: The candidate results distinguish Lean proofs, source tests, actual compiled-context evaluation and connected ledger execution. Removing source changes compiled identities, so earlier comparisons and receipts remain historical evidence. No source or build check establishes ledger acceptance or a budget bound.

evidence-and-limits.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/evidence-and-limits-02
evidence-and-limits.text: The pinned aiken docs reference is generated from the same source as the site. Each owner documents responsibility, dependencies, assumptions and invariants. The existing documentation checks reconcile public declarations with generated members and plant missing-documentation and stale-link faults. They establish presence and correspondence, not the truth of a behavioral claim. Read the validator API reference for every generated module.

the-current-contract.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/the-current-contract-01
the-current-contract.text: A registry integrator can register an unknown key and retire an active key permanently. The five other historical encodings are refused before approval or trie effects. The original broader source is archived on preserve/m2/pre-m1-source-removal; its custody and deletion paths are removed from the active source. Old deployed identities are refused, without migration.

the-current-contract.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/the-current-contract-02
the-current-contract.text: The boundary is fixed in the compiled state validator. Application approval alone is insufficient: caller-constructed requests, mint paths and mixed batches also pass through state admission. Witness policies require that state validator in the same transaction. Request rejection and retraction retain their applicable refund obligations; this carve does not settle the separate protected-rejection model question.

who-owns-a-state-validator-rule.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/who-owns-a-state-validator-rule-00
who-owns-a-state-validator-rule.text: Who owns a state validator rule.

who-owns-a-state-validator-rule.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/who-owns-a-state-validator-rule-01
who-owns-a-state-validator-rule.text: A contributor changing a registry rule wants one source owner beside the behavior it enforces. The active contract has one admission boundary, one fold, and one settlement path. This page maps those responsibilities and names the verification each change needs.

names-that-must-stay-distinct.name: docs-overview/names-that-must-stay-distinct-01
names-that-must-stay-distinct.text: Creating a request UTxO, minting an application action token, and minting a representative NFT are different events. A transaction constructing an Update/Delete request moves the representative that already exists; it does not mint a replacement representative.

registry-states.name: docs-overview/registry-states-01
registry-states.text: An absent key is available for Insert. Active means its representative NFT is outstanding, either in application custody or in a pending Update/Delete request. It does not mean the application is usable, unpaused or in any particular business state. Over permanently reserves the key with no live representative.

registry-states.name: docs-overview/registry-states-02
registry-states.text: Both stored values are payload-free. Application history or checkpoints needed for later application behavior must remain authenticated outside these values. No mapping of KERI close, pause or conviction to Singular operations is selected here.

registry-states.name: docs-overview/registry-states-03
registry-states.text: Continue with the lifecycle and certification.

responsibilities-and-terminology.name: docs-overview/responsibilities-and-terminology-01
responsibilities-and-terminology.text: Historical design. This page records the earlier Insert/Update/Delete design and its broader broader model successor. The active permanent permanent contract model supports only insertActive and updateTerminal. Historical tags 0, 2, 4, 5 and 6 encode refused actions, not available features. Current supported behavior describes permanent contract; archived source and evidence remain on preserve/m2/pre-m1-source-removal.

responsibilities-and-terminology.name: docs-overview/responsibilities-and-terminology-02
responsibilities-and-terminology.text: Singular maintains unique representative NFTs and the lifecycle of their registry keys. Applications maintain their own state and decide which application transitions are legal. MPF provides the authenticated registry data structure and proof mechanics.

what-each-layer-owns.name: docs-overview/what-each-layer-owns-01
what-each-layer-owns.text: Singular has no native owner, privileged requester or privileged folder. Permissionless submission does not mean arbitrary requests are valid. Applications can impose their own validation conditions; they cannot authorize bypassing Singular's NFT supply or custody rules.

choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.name: docs-payload-json/choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting-00
choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.text: Choose the form with the schema setting.

choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.name: docs-payload-json/choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting-01
choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.text: The setting has two values, plain and detailed, and plain when it is absent. It is not a standing setting: there is no environment variable and no key in the configuration file, because the form is a property of the file you give.

choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.name: docs-payload-json/choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting-02
choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.text: The refusal of a detailed file covers the whole document only. A detailed-looking object nested inside a larger document is plain JSON like any other: the file {"wrapper": {"int": 5}} is stored as a map from the text wrapper to a map from the text int to the integer 5. Every file the previous release accepted is therefore either refused with the instruction or read exactly as before when the setting is detailed; none is stored as a different datum.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-01
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: Reading a file in the plain schema turns its JSON into Plutus data by these rules, and by nothing else, so you can apply them by hand.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-02
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: A whole number becomes the integer. A number written 1.0 or 5e2 is a whole number too and is stored as 1 and 500; the way the number was written is not kept. A number may have at most a thousand digits.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-03
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: A text becomes the byte string of its UTF-8. The empty text is the empty byte string.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-04
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: true becomes the constructor with index 1 and no fields, which is the Plutus boolean, and false becomes the constructor with index 0 and no fields.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-05
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: An array becomes the list of its items, mapped in order. The empty array is the empty list.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-06
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: An object becomes the map from each key, as a byte string of its UTF-8, to its value, mapped. The entries are in ascending order of the key bytes, whatever order the file wrote them in. The empty object is the empty map.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-07
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: null and a number with a fraction are refused.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-08
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: A whole file is accepted, not only an object: the file may hold 42, "alice" or [1, 2].

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-09
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: Worked by hand, the file {"answer": 42} holds one object with one key, so the data is a map with one entry. The key is the byte string of the text answer, whose bytes are 616e73776572 in hex, and the value is the integer 42. In the detailed schema that is {"map":[{"k":{"bytes":"616e73776572"},"v":{"int":42}}]}. The file 42 is the integer 42, the same data as the detailed {"int":42}.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-01
limits.text: null is not stored. A later release may accept it without changing what is stored today.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-02
limits.text: The text of a number is not kept: 1.0 is read back as 1.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-03
limits.text: An object's key order in the file is not kept; the stored order is ascending by key bytes, because JSON readers do not preserve it and a map in Plutus data is ordered. A key repeated in the file keeps its first value, as the JSON reader does.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-04
limits.text: A payload with a byte string that is not text, a map with keys that are not text or any constructor other than the two booleans needs the detailed schema, and it prints in the detailed schema.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-05
limits.text: A text stored as bytes by the detailed schema reads back as text when the bytes are valid UTF-8; nobody can tell from the chain which form wrote it.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-06
limits.text: A whole payload that looks like a detailed document, such as {"int": 5} as a plain object, cannot be written in the plain schema because of the refusal above. It can be stored through the detailed schema as a map with the text key, and it then reads back as plain JSON; writing that JSON again needs the detailed form.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-07
limits.text: The settings table in connecting singular to a ledger provider lists --payload and --payload-schema with the commands that take them.

store-a-document.text: Write the file and give it to insert, with no other setting:

store-a-document.name: docs-payload-json/store-a-document-02
store-a-document.text: The second command prints the payload you wrote and the name of the schema it is printed in:

store-a-document.text: update takes the same file and the same setting, and so do the previews of both, keri-stub register, and the negative host's insert and update: every command that reads a payload file reads it one way.

store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.name: docs-payload-json/store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload-00
store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.text: Store ordinary JSON as a key's payload.

store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.name: docs-payload-json/store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload-01
store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.text: As a reader with a registry and a key, you store the document {"answer": 42} under the key by writing that file and nothing else. You read the key back and the page shows {"answer": 42}. You did not have to learn first how Plutus data is written in JSON. As an integrator who needs exact control of the bytes on chain, you keep writing the detailed schema, {"constructor": 0, "fields": [{"int": 42}]}, and say so on the command, so nothing is guessed. As someone with a script from the previous release, you find that your payload file in the detailed schema is refused with a sentence that tells you to say so, and is never stored as something else.

store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.name: docs-payload-json/store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload-02
store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.text: The first diagram shows how a file is read. The setting --payload-schema decides how the file becomes Plutus data: by the plain mapping of this page when the setting is plain or absent, and by the detailed schema, as before, when it is detailed. Either way the result is the same kind of value, Plutus data in the key's output on chain.

store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.name: docs-payload-json/store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload-03
store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.text: The second diagram shows how a key is read back. The data is printed as plain JSON if it has a plain reading and in the detailed schema if it has none, and the print always says which.

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-01
what-inspect-prints.text: inspect prints the key's payload under payload in the application output, with the field payloadSchema beside it, and the update receipt prints the two fields the same way. A payload has a plain reading when it is one that the rules above could have produced:

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-02
what-inspect-prints.text: an integer of at most a thousand digits;

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-03
what-inspect-prints.text: a byte string that is valid UTF-8, read as a text;

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-04
what-inspect-prints.text: a list whose items all have a plain reading;

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-05
what-inspect-prints.text: a map whose keys are valid UTF-8 byte strings in strictly ascending order of bytes and whose values all have a plain reading;

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-06
what-inspect-prints.text: the constructor with index 0 or 1 and no fields, read as false or true.

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-07
what-inspect-prints.text: When the stored data has a plain reading, payload is that JSON and payloadSchema is plain. Otherwise payload is the detailed schema of the data and payloadSchema is detailed: a byte string that is not text, a map with a key that is not text or with its keys out of order, any other constructor, or a number past the limit of a thousand digits.

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-08
what-inspect-prints.text: The reading is a property of the data, not of how it was stored. The detailed {"int":42} and the plain 42 store the same data, so both read back as 42. The envelope, with its control and its payload in the detailed schema, is printed as before under envelope, and it is the way to read the exact data.

what-is-refused.name: docs-payload-json/what-is-refused-01
what-is-refused.text: A refusal names the file, says what it asked for, and names the value and where it is, written as a path from the document: $ is the whole document, .name an object key and [2] an item. Every refusal comes before the node is read, so a preview with an unreachable node shows them too, and nothing is submitted.

what-is-refused.name: docs-payload-json/what-is-refused-02
what-is-refused.text: A number is judged by its size before it is written out, so a file such as 1e1000000000 is refused at once and the refusal names the number.

coverage-boundary.name: docs-prior-art/coverage-boundary-01
coverage-boundary.text: These candidates warrant component-level evaluation once a reuse target is concrete. License compatibility, toolchain fit and correctness require their own checks; this comparison grants none of them. Reading a validator establishes what its source says, not what a deployment does. Singular remains a design with unimplemented conformance obligations. Continue with the naming walkthrough or protocol specification.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-01
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: AdaDomains. The whitepaper, sections 3–4 describes separate registry/domain state, pooled requests and address changes. Section 3.1 puts the list of minted domains in the datum of a one-shot registry token; section 3.3 records the two limits that follow — one minting transaction per registry per block, and roughly 1600 short domains before the 16kB transaction limit binds; section 4.1 answers them by hashing names and splitting registries dynamically, and section 4.2 by a pooling layer in which the user who triggers minting must mint every pooled request belonging to that registry. Project resolution documentation describes reading the domain datum. The inspected resolver SDK at 302235c supplies resolution code. These establish architectural precedent and a public resolver, not an inspected generic registry implementation. A root-hash map moves that size limit off the key set, but it does not decide Singular's batch policy, which remains an open decision. Historical throughput assertions are not adopted here.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-02
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: ADA Handle DeMi. At 1b5623c, mint/burn validation traverses MPF proofs and checks an allowed minter. The check is symmetric: can_mint_demi_handles requires the selected allowed_minter among the signatories, and can_burn_demi_handles requires any settings minter, so deletion from the root is gated exactly as issuance is. Order validation supplies execution, cancellation and refund conditions, including a distinct-output binding that prevents one owner output from satisfying several refunds. Mechanical overlap is useful; replacing application and governor rules is substantive work.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-03
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: Distributed Set. The validator at 4b0547a and utilities authenticate set changes with current mint/withdrawal invocation. The set is a linked list of sorted-value nodes, each holding its own node NFT, rather than a hashed map: its state lives in as many UTxOs as it has nodes, and a node is split when it grows. Its plain spend branch checks sortedness, the head and tail anchors, the node NFT and the unchanged datum fields, and carries a TODO where a check that existing values survive would go — so membership preservation rests entirely on the configured mint or stake script, not on the set validator. The sources also target the pre-cardano/transaction Aiken standard library, which reuse would have to migrate. They do not supply Singular's prior-action receipt and NFT custody lifecycle.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-04
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: CIP113. At 1e83ed9, the registry, issuance policy and programmable base provide relevant authentication and policy-binding techniques: a key must be the policy ID derived from the issuance template parameterised with its minting logic, registration requires that logic's withdraw-0, and custody is dispatched through a credential read live from the protocol-params datum. The registry's redeemers are RegistryInit and RegistryInsert, and its spend handler admits a node NFT mint only with a positive amount, otherwise requiring a continuing output — a registered key is never removed. Their live delegation and custody contract would require substantive adaptation.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-05
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: Masumi. The registry-v2 mint policy at ce96026 addresses generated asset identities and versioning: an asset name is a nonce byte, the hash of a consumed output reference and a three-byte version, an update burns a token and mints its successor at version plus one, and a burn needs only possession. That is a different uniqueness problem from a registry of application-selected keys; no shared state records which keys are taken.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-06
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: CIP89's beacon pattern is also relevant precedent for minting that certifies an application UTxO: a beacon is minted only into a valid application output, burned when that output is spent, and never circulates. Singular's representative is the opposite in one respect that matters — it is held, moved between an application's own successive outputs, and carried into a terminal request — so the beacon rule cannot be adopted as stated, only its minting-time certification. A complete uniqueness, request and retirement protocol remains additional work.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-01
mpfs.text: MPFS is the nearest system to Singular and the one whose reuse must be answered explicitly, because Singular's map layer is MPF and the protocol specification already records, among its open decisions on transaction shapes and libraries, that old MPFS proofs are not proof of Singular's protocol. It is also the one candidate built as a component rather than as somebody's application: a cage is created by whoever consumes the seed, carries no application-specific rule, and serves whatever that creator puts in it. That posture is the one Singular copies. The difference is a single design decision inside it.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-02
mpfs.text: The inspected on-chain revision is cardano-mpfs-onchain at 34a5bfb. A cage is one NFT locked at the script address whose datum carries the MPF root. state.ak mints the cage token from a consumed seed, folds pending requests into a new root under Modify, and burns the cage under End. request.ak governs request UTxOs with Contribute, Retract and Sweep. shared.ak holds the authorization and phase predicates, and types.ak defines the request record and the map operations.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-03
mpfs.text: Four facts from that source decide the comparison.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-04
mpfs.text: Every spend of the state UTxO runs validateOwnership before the redeemer is examined, and that function requires the datum's single owner verification key hash among the transaction's signatories. Both Modify and End sit behind it.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-05
mpfs.text: Map entries are Operation values over ByteArray: Insert(value), Delete(value), Update(old, new). The cage mints exactly one token — its own state NFT — and no token is minted, burned or moved per key.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-06
mpfs.text: A request carries requestToken, requestOwner, the key, the operation, a tip and submitted_at. It commits to no application policy, no output shape and no approval; the only requester-side authorization anywhere in the validators is the Retract signature.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-07
mpfs.text: Requests are governed by time. Contribute requires Phase 1 or rejectability, Retract requires the requester's signature inside Phase 2, and Sweep lets the owner clear any request that is not processable against the current state.

prior-art-and-reuse-candidates.name: docs-prior-art/prior-art-and-reuse-candidates-01
prior-art-and-reuse-candidates.text: Comparison date: 2026-09-09. Implementation links pin revisions; website and whitepaper references record the material inspected on that date. Every source cited below was fetched at its pinned revision and read against the claim it supports.

prior-art-and-reuse-candidates.name: docs-prior-art/prior-art-and-reuse-candidates-02
prior-art-and-reuse-candidates.text: The inspected projects provide substantial precedent for Singular's architecture and mechanics. No ready-made implementation of its complete contract was established in this bounded comparison. This is not a novelty claim, security audit or exhaustive search. Source inspection does not establish deployed behavior.

retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.name: docs-prior-art/retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key-00
retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.text: Retirement and reuse of a key.

retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.name: docs-prior-art/retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key-01
retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.text: Singular needs two ways for a registration to end, and the distinction is what makes the lifecycle worth managing centrally. Delete burns the representative and returns the key to absence, so a later approved Insert may register it again. Update burns the representative and writes Over, which is terminal: the key is retired permanently and no later Insert can revive it. Permanent retirement is the requirement that came from Singular's first consumer, where an identity must be able to end without its name being reissued to someone else.

retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.name: docs-prior-art/retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key-02
retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.text: That requirement is not local to this project. CIP113 arrives at the same permanence from the other direction: its registry nodes are inserted and updated but never removed, so every registration it accepts is permanent whether or not permanence was wanted. Distributed Set leaves removal to the configured hook and specifies neither mode. MPFS supplies Delete, which frees the key, and nothing that retires one. No inspected system offers both modes under one contract, chosen per transition by the application that owns the entry.

the-authenticated-map-layer.name: docs-prior-art/the-authenticated-map-layer-01
the-authenticated-map-layer.text: This layer is the one part of Singular with ready implementations. The Aiken merkle-patricia-forestry library supplies on-chain proof verification, and is what both DeMi and MPFS build on; haskell-mts supplies the matching off-chain trie, proof generation and persistent storage. Choosing among these, or a different authenticated-set representation, does not resolve any of the open decisions, which are about certification, custody and retirement, not about how membership is proved.

what-remains-reusable-from-mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/what-remains-reusable-from-mpfs-01
what-remains-reusable-from-mpfs.text: The map layer and its off-chain machinery transfer; the authorization model does not. The fold shape — one proof per request applied against successive roots — is the shape Singular's permissionless fold requires. Off-chain, cardano-mpfs-offchain at 0f82465 supplies a cage indexer, a proof-bearing REST API, client transaction builders and cross-target verifiers over the same trie. Component-level reuse still needs its own evaluation: none of it was written against Singular's request or custody rules, and the decision on transaction shapes and shared libraries remains open.

what-singular-is-trying-to-be.name: docs-prior-art/what-singular-is-trying-to-be-00
what-singular-is-trying-to-be.text: What Singular is trying to be.

what-singular-is-trying-to-be.name: docs-prior-art/what-singular-is-trying-to-be-01
what-singular-is-trying-to-be.text: Singular is a component, not an application. A third party supplies one parameter — its application policy ID — and receives its own registry of unique keys with the representative NFT lifecycle managed end to end: minted into a certified application output on Insert, burned on retirement, burned and the key made available again on Delete. Nothing about the keys, the application's state or its business rules belongs to Singular.

what-singular-is-trying-to-be.name: docs-prior-art/what-singular-is-trying-to-be-02
what-singular-is-trying-to-be.text: That is the axis on which the prior art has to be read, and most of it fails before authorization is reached. A registry welded to one application is not reusable by anyone else at any price short of forking and rewriting it; the code inspected below is mostly of that kind, however good it is at its own job. MPFS is the exception and the model: it is application-agnostic, anyone may create a cage, and its single blocking difference from Singular is that every cage has an owner.

what-singular-is-trying-to-be.name: docs-prior-art/what-singular-is-trying-to-be-03
what-singular-is-trying-to-be.text: Two further layers are worth keeping apart. The authenticated-map layer — a key set whose whole state fits in one datum and whose changes are proved on-chain — has working implementations that Singular can adopt; an equivalent registry would not be disqualified merely because it uses a different authenticated-set representation. The registry contract layer — who may change the map, what an entry certifies about an application output, and what token custody is coupled to a transition — is where every inspected system diverges.

why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged.name: docs-prior-art/why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged-00
why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged.text: Why Singular cannot adopt MPFS unchanged.

why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged.name: docs-prior-art/why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged-01
why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged.text: The phase design is worth separating from the verdict. MPFS uses time windows to keep the oracle's fold and the requester's retraction from racing, which is a real solution to a problem Singular shares. It is unavailable here for the same reason the rest is: the windows are exclusive to a named oracle, and Singular has none. In its place, Singular resolves races inside the fold — an Insert is checked against absence in the applicable successive registry state, and admission of a request asserts nothing about the key.

checks-and-model-boundary.name: docs-record-value/checks-and-model-boundary-01
checks-and-model-boundary.text: Run just record-value-test from offchain/ to execute the production blueprint against an accepted maintain and named extra-asset refusals. The contexts are component fixtures, not submitted ledger transactions or a connected lifecycle. The same check runs in the naming validator CI job. The Aiken suite has the three issue reproductions and controls for added, removed, replaced and increased assets, ADA top-up, and insert-fold pollution.

checks-and-model-boundary.name: docs-record-value/checks-and-model-boundary-02
checks-and-model-boundary.text: Run nix flake check from naming-onchain/ for the Aiken suite and compiled identity checks. Root nix develop --quiet -c just ci covers the model, simulator, browser and documentation; it does not execute the offchain suites.

checks-and-model-boundary.name: docs-record-value/checks-and-model-boundary-03
checks-and-model-boundary.text: Lean is unchanged at repository revision 41861a66b72a840042f2e633ce33a607e817d6c6. Its Singular.Output models one representative plus scalar value. The implementation checks discharge that representation boundary for genuine insert-fold records and their continuations; the mapping is recorded in offchain/naming-correspondence.md.

deployment-compatibility.name: docs-record-value/deployment-compatibility-01
deployment-compatibility.text: With this rule the application validator hash is 1239f396899f80b7ec377fe181e2014b7bc54da0a4c4ab0d9df3fdc5. Before it, the hash was 89409890d5a89debf410d6d31695fc9030fcf2b754b06206d7291370, which is the one the preprod record carries, because that deployment predates the rule. Its spend and mint purposes share that identity. The committed naming-onchain/script-identity.json is regenerated from the pinned Aiken build, which retains user-defined traces. Other unapplied validator hashes stay the same.

deployment-compatibility.name: docs-record-value/deployment-compatibility-02
deployment-compatibility.text: The next deployment must derive its addresses and applied policies from the new blueprint. The representative policy's application-hash parameter changes with that deployment. The rule does not migrate records at an old script address, change an existing deployment manifest, or deploy to preprod.

for-a-names-controller.name: docs-record-value/for-a-names-controller-01
for-a-names-controller.text: An unrelated token in wallet change must not disable recovery or retirement. Naming records created by an insert fold contain exactly ADA and their representative. Maintain and recover require identical non-ADA policies, asset names and quantities in the continuation. ADA can increase, but cannot decrease.

when-a-value-is-refused.name: docs-record-value/when-a-value-is-refused-01
when-a-value-is-refused.text: record-value-preservation means a maintain or recover continuation changed its non-ADA value, or reduced its ADA. Keep wallet change in a separate output. record-single-asset means recovery or retirement encountered an input with zero or multiple non-ADA assets, or an insert fold tried to create a record without exactly its representative. These names are retained in compiled validator traces. The recovery and retirement runners also inspect all asset policies when reading a record, so they cannot hide an unrelated token.

when-a-value-is-refused.name: docs-record-value/when-a-value-is-refused-02
when-a-value-is-refused.text: An already polluted record can still be maintained if its entire non-ADA value is preserved. It cannot be repaired, recovered or retired under this rule. An arbitrary transfer to the script address is not a genuine naming registration.

how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.name: docs-recovery-retirement/how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry-00
how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.text: How a name moves in the registry.

how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.name: docs-recovery-retirement/how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry-01
how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.text: Naming is an instance of the registry, not a layer bolted beside it: a name is one key whose value is a single byte — Absent, Active or Terminal — and two supported registry requests move a key, each one moving a witness token. The naming walkthrough states the archived state table and witness laws once; this page shows application recovery and registry retirement as historical ledger evidence.

how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.name: docs-recovery-retirement/how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry-02
how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.text: The rule this page is about is naming's own: ending a name needs the committed recovery key or the retirement quorum, and never the current control key alone. The naming validator enforces it before the request reaches the fold, by certifying the edge in advance; the fold itself asks no application to sign.

how-retirement-ends-a-name.name: docs-recovery-retirement/how-retirement-ends-a-name-01
how-retirement-ends-a-name.text: Ending a name needs the committed recovery key or the retirement quorum — never the current control key alone. A thief holding the everyday control key and the holder themselves are indistinguishable to the chain, so if the current key could end a name, the thief could end it and recovery would arrive too late. The recovery route is the same proof recovery itself uses: reveal the preimage of the stored commitment, and sign with that address's payment key.

how-retirement-ends-a-name.name: docs-recovery-retirement/how-retirement-ends-a-name-02
how-retirement-ends-a-name.text: Run the ending rows against a real devnet node from offchain/ — the same retained-legacy status applies here as above: the retirement row runner stays declared and shipped, is not currently buildable or verified against the released source, and its re-cut is owned by #172. The usage is kept so the ending route stays documented, not as a claim you can run it today:

how-retirement-ends-a-name.name: docs-recovery-retirement/how-retirement-ends-a-name-03
how-retirement-ends-a-name.text: The private shallow TMPDIR keeps the devnet node database away from other work on the same host and keeps its socket inside the address length limit. The blueprint comes from the checked-out commit at run time; no store path is baked in and no dev shell is used.

how-retirement-ends-a-name.name: docs-recovery-retirement/how-retirement-ends-a-name-04
how-retirement-ends-a-name.text: Two failure controls shipped with the same runner. Making a refused row actually valid must fail the run, and matching refusals against an impossible marker must fail naming what came back:

how-retirement-ends-a-name.name: docs-recovery-retirement/how-retirement-ends-a-name-05
how-retirement-ends-a-name.text: Both exit non-zero by design, after executing rows.

limits-and-next-steps.name: docs-recovery-retirement/limits-and-next-steps-01
limits-and-next-steps.text: The active witness is a real token minted under the registry’s pinned active policy by the fold, and burned exactly once at completion; the registry binding on ledger is the state policy and token read from the spent state. Retirement custody is created and filled by authorized retires and spent only by permissionless completion (exact burn plus genuine registry transition) — withdrawal without burn, burn without transition, mismatched request pairings and re-registration after the name is Terminal all refuse, each attributed to its reason. No quorum rotation, no takeover, and no death oracle: the chain verifies authority, not death.

what-the-quorum-cannot-fix.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-quorum-cannot-fix-01
what-the-quorum-cannot-fix.text: Two weaknesses of the quorum are deliberate in this version, and stated here so that anybody choosing one knows what they are choosing.

what-the-quorum-cannot-fix.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-quorum-cannot-fix-02
what-the-quorum-cannot-fix.text: The quorum is fixed for the life of the name. No action rewrites it after booking. A member who loses their key, disappears, or turns hostile is a permanent member. The only route to a different quorum is to end the name and book it again — which means the name itself does not survive the change.

what-the-quorum-cannot-fix.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-quorum-cannot-fix-03
what-the-quorum-cannot-fix.text: The quorum can end the name while the controller is present. Nothing checks that the holder is gone, unreachable or in trouble. A threshold of members can end a live name at any moment, and the holder's own key cannot stop them. The quorum is an ending authority, not a death oracle and not an inheritance mechanism: choose its members as people you would accept that from.

what-the-quorum-cannot-fix.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-quorum-cannot-fix-04
what-the-quorum-cannot-fix.text: Both are known, both are visible, and neither is a defect to be reported — they are the shape of the version you are running.

what-the-retirement-run-observes.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-retirement-run-observes-01
what-the-retirement-run-observes.text: The run creates records at the application validator, each carrying the single active witness under the registry's pinned active policy with a quorum of two distinct members at threshold two, then executes each row against the outcome its contract specifies. Every refusal is asserted as a phase-two script failure naming the application validator, except the replay, where the ledger itself refuses the consumed output. One line per row begins with the full row name.

what-the-retirement-run-observes.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-retirement-run-observes-02
what-the-retirement-run-observes.text: The accepted rows prove custody from the chain: after a recovery-key ending and after a quorum ending, the active witness is observed at the custody script address in the accepting transaction's own outputs, and the consumed record is observed gone from the application validator. Completion is permissionless: the pending registry update folds with the custody spend and the exact burn, empty required signers, one fresh fee witness outside every route.

what-the-retirement-run-observes.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-retirement-run-observes-03
what-the-retirement-run-observes.text: The refusals are single-defect mutants of those accepts. A row authorized by the current control key alone is refused — the row that used to accept, and the one this version deliberately retires. A row one distinct signature short of the threshold is refused, and is otherwise exactly the accepted shape. A sibling row stores a quorum that names one member twice and a second once at threshold two — well-formed by the existing rules — with only the duplicated member signing: counting signatures instead of distinct members would accept it, so the row binds the distinctness the model demands. A reveal that is not the preimage of the stored commitment is refused on the same authorization.

what-the-retirement-run-observes.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-retirement-run-observes-04
what-the-retirement-run-observes.text: Ordinary maintenance carrying both quorum signatures and no controller signature is refused on the controller signature by the existing path, without any new check: the quorum can end a name and cannot steer it. A row authorized properly but sending the active witness anywhere but the custody script is refused on the ending request. The replay replays a real accepted ending against the record the chain no longer has, and the ledger itself refuses the spent output — recorded as exactly that, not dressed up as a validator refusal. After the refusals the surviving record is read back unchanged.

what-the-run-observes.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-run-observes-01
what-the-run-observes.text: The run creates three records at the application validator, each carrying the single active witness, then executes each row against the outcome its contract specifies. Every refusal is asserted as a phase-two script failure naming the application validator. One line per row begins with the full row name.

what-the-run-observes.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-run-observes-02
what-the-run-observes.text: The accepted row installs the reveal with a fresh commitment and proves the handover from the chain: the successor is read back and its active witnesses, registry binding, payment destination and quorum are compared field by field against the pre-recovery values, its control address is compared against the reveal, and its commitment is shown fresh and different. Its required signers are exactly the revealed payment key.

what-the-run-observes.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-run-observes-03
what-the-run-observes.text: The refusals are single-defect mutants of the accepted row. A different reveal signed by its own key, a replay of the consumed reveal against the genuine successor, and a stored digest computed without the domain separation are refused on the commitment. A correct reveal with no signer, and the same reveal signed by the old controller, are refused on the required signer. A successor that re-installs the consumed commitment is refused on the fresh commitment. A record carrying anything but its single active witness, a claim naming a different registry binding, and a successor altering the quorum are refused on the record’s shape, the registry, and field preservation. Successors that change the payment destination or install a controller other than the reveal are refused on field preservation as further sub-cases of the same row. After a real accepted row, the old controller's ordinary maintenance is refused on the controller signature, and maintenance under the recovered controller succeeds, proving the name remains usable. After the refusals the records are read back unchanged.

what-the-run-observes.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-the-run-observes-04
what-the-run-observes.text: The commitment is BLAKE2b-256("singular/naming/next-control/v1" || 0x00 || canonical-address-bytes) over the whole binary address including header and network. Only canonical base and enterprise addresses with payment-key credentials are supported.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-you-can-do-00
what-you-can-do.text: What you can do.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-you-can-do-01
what-you-can-do.text: The recovery row runner is a retained legacy command of the current release: it stays declared and shipped, but it is not currently buildable or verified against the released source, and its re-cut against the current registry mode is owned by #172. Its usage is kept below so the page stays faithful to what these rows did — not as a claim you can run it today. When it was current, it ran the eleven recovery rows against a real devnet node from offchain/:

what-you-can-do.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-you-can-do-02
what-you-can-do.text: The private shallow TMPDIR keeps the devnet node database away from other work on the same host and keeps its socket inside the address length limit. The blueprint comes from the checked-out commit at run time; no store path is baked in and no dev shell is used.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-you-can-do-03
what-you-can-do.text: Two failure controls shipped with the same runner. Making a refused row actually valid must fail the run, and matching refusals against an impossible marker must fail naming what came back:

what-you-can-do.name: docs-recovery-retirement/what-you-can-do-04
what-you-can-do.text: Both exit non-zero by design, after executing rows.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-recovery-retirement/who-this-is-for-00
who-this-is-for.text: Who this is for.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-recovery-retirement/who-this-is-for-01
who-this-is-for.text: A holder of an active name who has lost the everyday control key and planned ahead by committing to a next controller in advance. This page shows how that holder spends the record with the address committed to earlier, signs with that address's payment key alone, and sees the chain hand over control — then maintains the name normally under the new key while the old key stops working.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-recovery-retirement/who-this-is-for-02
who-this-is-for.text: It is also for a holder who wants to end a name permanently, and for the quorum fixed at registration that can end it without the holder. Ending a name needs the committed recovery key or that quorum — the everyday control key alone cannot do it. Either route moves the active witness into completion-only custody, a script with no withdrawal path, and neither route can be turned into a takeover or a payment redirection.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-recovery-retirement/who-this-is-for-03
who-this-is-for.text: The ledger receipts described below belong to the archived broader source. The current two-edge model retains the applicable application maintenance, recovery and retirement rules, but those historical receipts do not certify the revised compiled candidate. See current candidate results.

book-a-registration.name: docs-registry-commands/book-a-registration-01
book-a-registration.text: As Alice, you book a key with its payload and a deposit under a registry you name by its address, and the registry's configuration decides the deadlines.

book-a-registration.name: docs-registry-commands/book-a-registration-02
book-a-registration.text: The booking puts a pending registration at the request address of open datum. It holds the deposit (2 000 000 lovelace unless --deposit says more; a deposit below the minimum ADA of the output that will hold the key's token with its payload is refused, naming that minimum), the tip for whoever folds it (--tip, nothing by default), and its approval, the token that a fold, a reclaim or a cleanup consumes. The payload is the file --payload names, read in the form --payload-schema gives, plain JSON unless you say otherwise; store ordinary JSON as a key's payload gives the rules. --refund-address says where a reclaim or a cleanup returns the value, and it is your own address when you do not say.

book-a-registration.name: docs-registry-commands/book-a-registration-03
book-a-registration.text: The receipt names the pending registration, its approval, the key, the deposit, the tip, the refund address and the three times that matter: when it was booked, its processing deadline, and the end of its reclaim window. Whoever folds it, or you taking it back, names the pending registration with --pending.

book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.name: docs-registry-commands/book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it-00
book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.text: Book permanent termination, then fold it.

book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.name: docs-registry-commands/book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it-01
book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.text: As Alice, you choose your live holding and book permanent termination. Its protected deposit is donated to the treasury in this transaction. The new request has no datum and holds exactly the active token and one termination approval; its ADA is the reward available to the folder. The active token moves into this request and is not burned at booking. There is no reclaim or cancellation window for this booking.

book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.name: docs-registry-commands/book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it-02
book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.text: The receipt names the pending output and the treasuryDonation in lovelace. As Bob, you fold that pending output with open-datum state fold, using --pending TXID#IX and your own vault. You need the public chain and your wallet; Alice's key, local directory and records are unnecessary. The fold burns the active token and the approval, creates no replacement holding, and leaves the key terminal permanently. You receive the request's whole value; your ordinary wallet input pays the transaction fee. A batch may mix terminations with registrations of other keys. A termination has no processing deadline.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-01
create-a-registry.text: As Carol, you spend one output of your wallet to make a registry, and the output you spend fixes the registry's identity.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-02
create-a-registry.text: The second diagram shows what a creation does. The command reads your wallet and looks for live reference copies of the validators. The first registry of an application publishes each in its own transaction, state first, and waits for both before it creates the registry. If you stop between publications, a rerun finds the live copy and publishes only the missing script. A later registry finds both live copies and sends one transaction. The registry's state token appears on the first output of the creation, and the command reads it back before it prints the receipt.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-03
create-a-registry.text: open-datum state create makes a registry of open datum. Five parameters are fixed here for the life of the registry: the processing time and the reclaim time of a booked registration (--process-time and --reclaim-time), the widest validity interval a booking may declare (--booking-width), and the registration cost and the minimum tip (--registration-cost and --minimum-tip), which the registry carries and nothing enforces.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-04
create-a-registry.text: singular state create makes the registry of any application whose policy you give with --application-policy: the policy is the one parameter of the state validator. The command publishes the state validator when no live copy of it exists, and creates the registry whose state token that validator guards.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-05
create-a-registry.text: The seed is your wallet's largest ada-only output, chosen when the registry is built and after the validators have been published when they had to be, so the publication cannot have spent it. --seed names another output of your wallet. The wallet funds the transactions and keeps their change. The builders choose the funding, so these commands refuse --fund-input, --max-outlay and --preview by name rather than ignore them.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-06
create-a-registry.text: The receipt names the registry's address and fingerprint, its state token, the seed, the output that now holds the state, the registry's root, the policy of the application, each validator with the output that carries its reference script and whether this command published it, and every transaction the command sent with what became of it.

create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on-the-proved-design-00
create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: Create a registry and manage its keys on the proved design.

create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on-the-proved-design-01
create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: As Carol, you create a registry for an application with one command and read its address and its state token from the receipt. As Alice, you book the registration of a key with its payload and a deposit, and the receipt names the pending registration the booking made. As Bob, you fold the registrations you name into the registry from the chain alone, and keep what each of them holds above its deposit. As Alice again, when nobody folds your registration you take it back inside its reclaim window, and when that window has passed anyone can clean it up and your deposit goes back to the refund address you chose. When a command is interrupted, the next write of the same wallet settles what it left, and nothing is ever sent a second time.

create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on-the-proved-design-02
create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: The first diagram shows the life of one registration. A booking makes it pending. Until its processing deadline only a fold can spend it. After the deadline, and until the reclaim window ends, only the refund address can take it back. After the window anyone can clean it up.

create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on-the-proved-design-03
create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: This page describes eight commands: singular state create, open-datum state create, open-datum state fold, open-datum registration book, open-datum registration reclaim and open-datum registration cleanup, open-datum holding update and open-datum holding terminate. Every flag they take is listed with its description and its default in the settings table, and each command prints the same information with --help.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-00
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: Fold registrations and terminations into the registry.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-01
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: As Bob, you fold the registrations you name into the registry in one transaction, and you need nothing from anyone who booked them.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-02
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: Each registration's approval is consumed and the key's token is minted into the holding the registration committed to. The fold is built from the chain alone, and the wallet that runs it keeps what each request holds above its deposit. Nothing is chosen for you: every registration is named with --pending, and a registration that cannot be folded refuses the command, saying why.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-03
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: The receipt names the registry's new root, the output that holds the state, and each registration folded with its key.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-00
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: Take a registration back, or clean it up.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-01
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: As Alice, you take back a registration you booked while its reclaim window is open.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-02
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: Everything the registration holds returns to its refund address, which must be the wallet that runs the command, and its approval is burned. Before the window opens or after it closes the command is refused, saying when.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-03
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: As anyone, you clean up an expired registration once its reclaim window has ended.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-04
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: The deposit returns to the refund address, the wallet that runs the command keeps what the request holds above the deposit, and the approval is burned. Both commands name exactly one pending registration.

update-a-live-holding.name: docs-registry-commands/update-a-live-holding-01
update-a-live-holding.text: As Alice, you choose the output that holds your active key and replace its payload. The control stays the same: its registry, active token, key, controller and protected deposit. The holding keeps all its tokens and at least the deposit. If the larger datum needs more minimum ADA, your wallet supplies it. No registry state is spent by the update.

update-a-live-holding.name: docs-registry-commands/update-a-live-holding-02
update-a-live-holding.text: The receipt names the new holding output. Use that reference for a later update or termination. A missing holding, another controller, or another named registry is refused before the transaction is signed.

when-a-command-is-interrupted.name: docs-registry-commands/when-a-command-is-interrupted-01
when-a-command-is-interrupted.text: As any of the three, you may lose the connection, stop the command, or run past --confirm-timeout. The command never sends a transaction twice.

when-a-command-is-interrupted.name: docs-registry-commands/when-a-command-is-interrupted-02
when-a-command-is-interrupted.text: The third diagram shows what happens to a transaction that was in flight. Every transaction is written to the journal under its identity before it is sent. If the command is interrupted, whatever the moment, the transaction keeps that identity. The next write of the same wallet for the same registry reads its journal before it builds anything. A transaction the chain holds is recorded as landed and named under reconciled in the next receipt, and a transaction the node refused stays recorded as refused. A transaction the chain does not yet show stops the next write, naming it, and nothing is built or sent until it is settled. A creation is journalled under the application and the wallet, because the name of the registry it makes is known only once its seed is chosen; the other commands are journalled under the registry.

when-a-command-is-interrupted.name: docs-registry-commands/when-a-command-is-interrupted-03
when-a-command-is-interrupted.text: --state-dir names the root of the journals, and the default is the per-user state directory. Recovering a registry command shows each of these interruptions on a development network.

where-the-keys-token-goes.name: docs-registry-commands/where-the-keys-token-goes-01
where-the-keys-token-goes.text: A registration commits, when it is booked, to the address that will hold its key's token once it is folded. open-datum registration book commits the request address of open datum. The fold accepts any address a registration committed to, the address of the state validator itself included. A token folded into a holding at the state validator's own address stays where only the state validator can spend it. That is the choice of whoever booked the registration, and the fold does not refuse it.

a-page-from-the-two-actor-run.name: docs-registry-page/a-page-from-the-two-actor-run-00
a-page-from-the-two-actor-run.text: A page from the two-actor run.

a-page-from-the-two-actor-run.name: docs-registry-page/a-page-from-the-two-actor-run-01
a-page-from-the-two-actor-run.text: Alice's page after her own fold, on the development network: the facts that run recorded, with the release it ran, version 0.10.1, as the command prints them now. A later release prints its own label:

a-page-from-the-two-actor-run.name: docs-registry-page/a-page-from-the-two-actor-run-02
a-page-from-the-two-actor-run.text: One active key, no terminal keys, one fold since create: Alice's own insertion, folded by her, read back under the fold's root.

read-it.name: docs-registry-page/read-it-01
read-it.text: From the extracted release archive, whose blueprint is onchain/plutus.json with the version.txt beside it, and with the state token:

read-it.name: docs-registry-page/read-it-02
read-it.text: The page prints as indented JSON, which a person reads and any JSON parser reads. A script takes a field by name:

read-it.name: docs-registry-page/read-it-03
read-it.text: The json switch is accepted and changes nothing, so a script that passes it keeps working:

read-it.name: docs-registry-page/read-it-04
read-it.text: The command takes the state token, the blueprint of the packaged release, a provider and a network. It takes no wallet, no signing key, no state directory and no file of any actor; any other setting is refused by name before anything is read. The version label comes from the version file beside the blueprint. From an extracted release archive, run the archive's own singular with its blueprint and the adjacent version file: the Demo 1 journey reads the page this way right after create, from the command the create receipt printed. A success prints the page alone and writes no file; every refusal prints one JSON receipt and exits non-zero.

read-it.name: docs-registry-page/read-it-05
read-it.text: The page carries no clock, no chain tip and no session identity, so identical inputs give identical bytes. Pending requests appear in one fixed order. With or without the json switch the page is the same bytes: the keys come in alphabetical order, as the encoder prints them, and the table above is the order of this page's sections, not of the keys.

read-the-registry-page-generated-from-th.name: docs-registry-page/read-the-registry-page-generated-from-the-chain-00
read-the-registry-page-generated-from-th.text: Read the registry page generated from the chain.

read-the-registry-page-generated-from-th.name: docs-registry-page/read-the-registry-page-generated-from-the-chain-01
read-the-registry-page-generated-from-th.text: As Alice, you hold a registry's state token and the packaged release, and nothing else: no wallet file of yours, nothing from the person who created the registry. You run one command and read which registry this is, which release it runs, what its rules are and what it holds now. As Bob, on your own machine, you run the same command: reading the same chain state with the same release gives you the same bytes. As a script, you read the page with an ordinary JSON parser and take its fields by name. As an integrator, you want to know what the page does not prove, and the page says so itself.

refusals.name: docs-registry-page/refusals-01
refusals.text: A refusal prints one JSON receipt on standard output with a non-zero exit status, as every command does.

the-registrys-pinned-policies.name: docs-registry-page/the-registrys-pinned-policies-01
the-registrys-pinned-policies.text: The registry section shows the two policies the registry's datum pins: the application and active policies. They are the registry's own statement, read from its state datum, and they never change after the registry is created. The command compares the active policy with the ones the release derives for this registry before it prints anything: a registry that pins another is refused, as the refusals below say.

the-registrys-pinned-policies.name: docs-registry-page/the-registrys-pinned-policies-02
the-registrys-pinned-policies.text: The application policy is the one the command cannot derive. The command is told the registry and the release, and the release does not say which application the registry was created for, so the application policy shown is the datum's own and the page says so beside it: the field applicationPin reads not-checked-against-any-blueprint. An application's own program, which knows its blueprint, derives the application policy as well and compares it, and its output reads compared. The page never presents a value read from the datum as if the release had derived it, and the release section holds only the release's own claims.

what-is-not-in-this-page.name: docs-registry-page/what-is-not-in-this-page-00
what-is-not-in-this-page.text: What is not in this page.

what-is-not-in-this-page.name: docs-registry-page/what-is-not-in-this-page-01
what-is-not-in-this-page.text: A block anchor for the last fold waits on its own provider read. The documentation links are computed from the claimed version, not checked against a published asset. The independently derived action identity in the public report waits on its own slice. None of these changes what the page shows; each arrives separately.

what-the-page-does-not-prove.name: docs-registry-page/what-the-page-does-not-prove-00
what-the-page-does-not-prove.text: What the page does not prove.

what-the-page-does-not-prove.name: docs-registry-page/what-the-page-does-not-prove-01
what-the-page-does-not-prove.text: The provenance field says it in fixed text: the page shows the public history of the state token from create to the live state output, each fold's rebuilt root checked against the root recorded in that fold's state datum, and nothing beyond it. The history was read from Koios. The provider's answers are unverified: raw facts and untrusted reconstruction material, no ledger proofs and no anchor. The release label is the archive's own claim. The page is unsigned.

ending-a-name.name: docs-retirement/ending-a-name-01
ending-a-name.text: The current contract permits registration and permanent retirement only. The retained command now checks an unknown key and an already terminal key against real accepting controls. Absent leaves cannot be created from permanent contract genesis; their retirement refusal is a synthetic compiled-context check. The following broader-model story and receipts are archived evidence, not current deployment support. See current candidate results.

seeing-it-happen.name: docs-retirement/seeing-it-happen-01
seeing-it-happen.text: The release archive ships a command that performs the whole story against a throwaway network, from a fresh extraction with no source checkout:

seeing-it-happen.name: docs-retirement/seeing-it-happen-02
seeing-it-happen.text: It boots a registry, books a name to a wallet, retires it, and writes what it saw to the file you name: the two transaction ids, the three registry roots, the token count going from one to zero, the exact burn, the input it came from, and the final entry. The two refusals are in there too, each beside a retirement that did work — because "it was refused" only means something when you can see the same machinery succeed on the next line.

seeing-it-happen.name: docs-retirement/seeing-it-happen-03
seeing-it-happen.text: Every value in that file is read back from the network or from the compiled contract. None of it is written by the command to make itself look right.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-00
what-you-can-do.text: What you can do.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-01
what-you-can-do.text: Retire a name you hold. The registry takes the token back out of your wallet and burns it, and the name's entry becomes Terminal — the last state it will ever have.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-02
what-you-can-do.text: What has to be true for it to go through:

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-03
what-you-can-do.text: the registry's entry for your key reads Active;

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-04
what-you-can-do.text: the transaction carries your token — the one the booking delivered — as an input for the burn to destroy;

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-05
what-you-can-do.text: nothing else moves under the registry's active token policy.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-06
what-you-can-do.text: What comes out:

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-07
what-you-can-do.text: exactly one token destroyed, the one named by your key, and no output anywhere carries it afterwards;

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-08
what-you-can-do.text: the entry reads Terminal;

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-09
what-you-can-do.text: no refund, no new token, and no signature from any application at the fold.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-retirement/what-you-can-do-10
what-you-can-do.text: The last point is worth stating plainly: the fold asks no application to sign a retirement. The registry decides, from the entry and the token, and nothing else. What an application can do is decide who may build the request in the first place. The naming instance does exactly that: ending a name needs the committed recovery key or the retirement quorum, never the current control key alone, and the naming validator refuses any other request before it exists to be folded. Recover control and retire names on a real ledger shows that rule enforced on chain.

when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-ma.name: docs-retirement/when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-matters-00
when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-ma.text: When it is refused, and why the reason matters.

when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-ma.name: docs-retirement/when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-matters-01
when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-ma.text: Three different situations look the same from outside — "the retirement did not happen" — and the registry keeps them apart, because the repair is different in each case:

when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-ma.name: docs-retirement/when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-matters-02
when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-ma.text: Each of these is decided against the registry's own entry, not against what the request claims about it. A request that says "this key is active" does not make it so, and a retirement built on that claim is refused by name rather than dying inside a proof.

when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-ma.name: docs-retirement/when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-matters-03
when-it-is-refused-and-why-the-reason-ma.text: The last row is different from the other three: under the registry's laws, an Active entry and exactly one outstanding token are the same fact, so a caller cannot actually reach that situation. It stays a guard because a guard that is never reached is cheap, and because being wrong about it would destroy nothing while claiming to.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-retirement/who-this-is-for-00
who-this-is-for.text: Who this is for.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-retirement/who-this-is-for-01
who-this-is-for.text: You hold a Singular name. You booked it, the registry handed you a token that says so, and now you want it over — permanently, publicly, and in a way nobody can undo, including you.

who-this-is-for.name: docs-retirement/who-this-is-for-02
who-this-is-for.text: This page is about that one move: retirement. It is the edge the registry calls updateTerminal: it burns the active witness and leaves the key where no edge can move it again. This is the registry edge on its own; the naming instance puts a rule of its own in front of it, stated below.

why-it-cannot-be-undone.name: docs-retirement/why-it-cannot-be-undone-01
why-it-cannot-be-undone.text: Terminal is the end of the line by construction. A second retirement at the same key does not produce a smaller effect or a no-op — it produces no transaction at all, refused terminal-immutable. There is no edge out of Terminal in the registry's table, so no sequence of folds returns the name to circulation.

why-it-cannot-be-undone.name: docs-retirement/why-it-cannot-be-undone-02
why-it-cannot-be-undone.text: That is also why the token is destroyed rather than parked somewhere: while a token exists, someone holds it, and "who holds it" is a question with consequences. After a retirement there is nothing to hold.

play-the-simulation.name: docs-simulation/play-the-simulation-01
play-the-simulation.text: Open the playable Singular simulator. It is one self-contained page: no framework, no network, no server. Everything it computes it computes in front of you.

play-the-simulation.name: docs-simulation/play-the-simulation-02
play-the-simulation.text: The page is a transcription of the frozen Lean model into JavaScript, so that a reader can play what the proofs are about. Where the two disagree the Lean is right and the page is a defect — which is exactly what the corpus replay on the page is for.

play-the-simulation.name: docs-simulation/play-the-simulation-03
play-the-simulation.text: The active engine now mirrors permanent permanent contract. Earlier absence, deletion and terminal-attestation journeys are retired; their encodings are refusal controls.

reproduce-the-checks.name: docs-simulation/reproduce-the-checks-01
reproduce-the-checks.text: From a source checkout, inside the development shell:

reproduce-the-checks.name: docs-simulation/reproduce-the-checks-02
reproduce-the-checks.text: just simulator runs three commands. node simulator/build.mjs --check rebuilds the standalone page from its sources and fails if the committed index.html differs, so the page you play is the page in the repository. node simulator/gate.mjs replays the corpus outside the browser and reports what it covered:

reproduce-the-checks.name: docs-simulation/reproduce-the-checks-03
reproduce-the-checks.text: The command reports computed row counts and labels each corpus section as executed behavior or inspected evidence. Registry cases and codecs are executed; request-exit payment rows, composed transaction rows, naming and lifecycle observations are inspected Lean evidence. This page has no request-exit engine. Five laws have applicable finite transition examples. Terminal immutability and terminal-attestation soundness retain Lean proofs but have no admitted-transition example with their terminal hypotheses; the page reports them as proved only.

reproduce-the-checks.name: docs-simulation/reproduce-the-checks-04
reproduce-the-checks.text: node simulator/gate.mjs --selftest then seeds a defect and requires the gate to reject it. A checker that has never been seen to fail is not evidence, so the failing run is part of the passing one.

reproduce-the-checks.name: docs-simulation/reproduce-the-checks-05
reproduce-the-checks.text: just browser loads the built page in Chromium, serves nothing but index.html — every other request returns 404, which is how the page's self-containment is checked rather than asserted — plays the journeys, drives free play including the wrong-tuple approval, reads the refusal table and verifies the naming journey. A page error or an outbound network request fails the run.

what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-no.name: docs-simulation/what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-not-00
what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-no.text: What the page proves, and what it does not.

what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-no.name: docs-simulation/what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-not-01
what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-no.text: Every case in the corpus carries its input — the state before and the request — not just the answer, so the page recomputes each one from scratch and compares. The header line on the page reports the count it actually reproduced against the count it was given; a page that silently skipped cases would show a smaller denominator, and one that skipped all of them would show zero rather than passing.

what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-no.name: docs-simulation/what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-not-02
what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-no.text: That establishes agreement on the exported inputs. It is not a proof of equivalence: a transcription can agree on every corpus row and still diverge on the next one. The proofs are in the Lean; the page is evidence that what you are playing is the thing that was proved about, over the cases the model itself chose to export.

what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-no.name: docs-simulation/what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-not-03
what-the-page-proves-and-what-it-does-no.text: One caveat a reader should have, stated plainly. The Lean model, the corpus generator and this transcription were written by the same author. Agreement between them is therefore weaker evidence than agreement between independent implementations would be: a misunderstanding held while writing the model is very likely to be held again while transcribing it. The corpus replay catches transcription slips, which is what it is for. It cannot catch a shared misreading of the specification. The independent check on that is the audit of the Lean statements against the interface, not this page.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-simulation/what-you-can-do-00
what-you-can-do.text: What you can do.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-simulation/what-you-can-do-01
what-you-can-do.text: Follow a journey. Seven stories: register a name, retire it permanently, and refuse each of the five excluded encodings. The retirement story also attempts to reuse the terminal key and observes key-exists. Registration mints an active token; retirement consumes it and leaves the key terminal.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-simulation/what-you-can-do-02
what-you-can-do.text: Step with ⏮ ◀ ▶ ⏭. Stepping back unwinds the tokens as well as the leaf, so you can watch a witness appear and disappear. Where a story reaches a point that admits more than one continuation, the branches are offered and taking one does not destroy the other.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-simulation/what-you-can-do-03
what-you-can-do.text: Try it yourself. Free play gives you the seven historical encodings: two supported edges and five refusals, a key, an owner, an output and a deposit, and a choice of approval: matching, right policy but wrong tuple, another policy, or none at all. The third and fourth are obviously refused. The second is the interesting one — an approval minted under the registry's own pinned policy, for a real request, that does not match this request's edge, key, owner and destination. It is refused, and a model that checked only the policy would admit it.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-simulation/what-you-can-do-04
what-you-can-do.text: Read what is refused, by name. Seven encoded operations against four possible leaves give twenty-eight combinations. Two are admissible transitions; twenty-six are refused. Unsupported tags return edge-inadmissible before approval or trie effects. Supported tags still check the matching approval, leaf and active-token presence. Synthetic absent leaves are unreachable from permanent contract genesis and are shown as invalid-context controls.

what-you-can-do.name: docs-simulation/what-you-can-do-05
what-you-can-do.text: See the naming instance. Switch to Naming — permanent retirement. The same engine registers and retires a name, then refuses terminal witnessing.
